# Session dispatch + babysitting (OpenChamber program)

## Purpose
Move the fleet's larger code work off Claude cron shifts — whose every turn re-buys a large context — onto OpenChamber-hosted OpenCode sessions running on plan pools, watched by ONE babysitter worker instead of one worker per issue. Design record: `openchamber-dispatch-babysitter-design-2026-10-26.md` (keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace, files/).

## Scope
- **Locations abstraction:** a session executor is a location (kind: openchamber | opencode-server | openclaw | codex-aster) with an adapter + capacity, so more OpenChamber machines, an OpenClaw gateway, or a Codex `.aster` route plug in without changing the babysitter loop. First location: the laptop's OpenChamber.
- **Dispatcher with admission control:** hands queue tasks marked `executor: openchamber` to sessions only when a slot is free and the routed pool passes the quota measurement gate; otherwise hands the task back (parked `executor-saturated`, noted on the issue) — never a silent backlog.
- **One babysitter:** rounds over every bound session — progress verdicts, one stall nudge then escalation, quota walls as named parks, harvesting finished sessions into verified terminal queue states. Reports quota per pool and a routing ledger (pool used per session, escalations, burn per landed task).
- **Routing, Workhorse-first:** Fast / Workhorse (default) / Frontier tiers per the POOL MAP; Frontier only on evidence or for the design half of a split
title: epic(openchamber): session dispatch + babysitting — OpenChamber as the fleet's workhorse executor

## Symptom

`openchamber session list --dir /home/user/git/code --limit 250 --with-status --json` fails with exit 1 in about 4 s, and the OpenChamber scheduled queue lanes stop before claiming. The runbook treats a failed same-lane overlap check as a stop, so every affected lane claims nothing.

## Evidence (2026-11-18, all times local)

- `oc-code-03` 02:42, `code-f` 02:40 (before the failure window), `oc-code-05` 02:50 and `oc-code-07` 02:58: the overlap check failed. The 02:50 and 02:58 runs report "timed out after 4 seconds".
- `code-g`, `code-i` and "Improvement issue creator — lane B" at 03:00 show directory `unknown-directory` in the session list.
- Rerun at about 03:10 by the advocate: still rc=1 after 4.2 s, with `--limit 5` too.
- The lanes stop cleanly, so no queue item is lost. The effect is idle scheduled capacity, not corruption.

## Suspected cause (unverified)

The OpenChamber control API that `session list` calls is not answering on the laptop, or `session list` errors on sessions whose directory is unknown. Only the first command's exit path has been checked, not the server logs.

## Ask

1. Reproduce `openchamber session list` on the laptop and capture stderr and the server log.
2. Decide whether the overlap check should fail open (claim with a warning) or stay fail-closed, and document the choice in the runbook.
3. Fix or document the `unknown-directory` case.

body:
## Problem

The pm-dispatch service answers HTTP 502 to both of its write endpoints, and has for at least four consecutive days. Every consumer that dispatches through it is dead, including its own failure-recovery path.

## Evidence (verified fresh 2026-11-08T00:25Z, gh run logs)

`Jules Daily Upstream Sync (OpenChamber)` in developing-today-forks/openchamber, scheduled runs on `main`:

- 2026-11-04 run 41828572424: `pm-dispatch-start: pm-dispatch POST /v1/sessions failed (HTTP 502)`; failure-queue step `POST /v1/tasks` also 502.
- 2026-11-05 run 42028456274: identical 502 pair.
- 2026-11-06 run 42216683583: identical 502 pair.
- 2026-11-07 run 42367237603: identical 502 pair.

Setup and checkout pass; the dispatch step is the first failure. Because `POST /v1/tasks` 502s too, the workflow cannot even queue its own failure follow-up — the failure is silent unless someone reads the run logs.

## Impact

- The daily upstream sync of developing-today-forks/openchamber has not run since 2026-11-03 (the Nov 3 run failed differently, on an Actions staging error that has not recurred; the workflow has since moved to local `./.github/actions/pm-dispatch-*` actions, which load fine).
- Tracked on the OpenChamber side as developing-today-forks/openchamber#1450 (queue task 7543, now at its attempt cap) and the workflow's own tracker developing-today-forks/openchamber#1570.
- Any other pm-dispatch consumer hitting `/v1/sessions` or `/v1/tasks` in this window presumably failed the same wa
title: pm-dispatch: POST /v1/sessions and /v1/tasks answer HTTP 502 — daily upstream sync dead since 2026-11-04

# Design mill: one fleet surface for OpenCode, OpenChamber, ID, and mcpx

Drew's design, dictated 2026-11-14. Protected design — do not close or drop without Drew.

## The idea in plain words

All automation and agent calls to OpenChamber, OpenCode, the ID binary, and the mcpx binary should go through subcommands of the fleet binary. At first this is mostly pass-through to the same underlying binary/endpoint, but fleet automatically resolves WHERE to talk: the right port on localhost, the right socket, the right endpoint path for that service on that host. Credentials are populated automatically and the caller can skip those fields. A raw mode (explicit endpoint path, raw POST body, explicit flag) always exists as an override.

This is a design mill with multiple passes, not one build. Passes are filed as sibling issues and cross-linked here.

## Cross-cutting rules Drew set

- Auto-resolution is the default; a specific flag overrides it. Defaults: the service's standard port on localhost or its socket.
- Endpoints can be customized per subprogram: a service may have a standard port, a website port, a homepage path, or a unique-ID custom path taken from settings, used raw.
- Everything exposed as a command should also be exposable as MCP and as REST (flag-gated, not all on at once). Later possibly GraphQL by the same switch.
- ID is the identity/transport layer of the whole system: many fleet commands will read/write the local or configured ID store, which may itself be remot

# Design mill pass 1: fleet subcommands for OpenCode, OpenChamber, ID, mcpx — pass-through with automatic endpoint + credential resolution

Part of the fleet-surface design mill (Drew, 2026-11-14). Parent issue cross-links all passes.

## What to design

Fleet gains subcommand families for each of the four tools (working names: `fleet opencode`, `fleet openchamber`, `fleet id`, `fleet mcpx`). In this first pass they mostly pass through to the same binary or endpoint as today — the value is that fleet owns resolution:

- **Endpoint resolution**: fleet knows each service's standard local endpoint (port on localhost, or unix socket) and uses it by default. Resolution is automatic unless the caller passes an explicit override flag.
- **Credential population**: when the target needs credentials, fleet fills them in from its normal secret routes; callers may omit those fields entirely.
- **Raw mode**: a caller can pass an exact endpoint path and a raw body (e.g. a raw POST) — the escape hatch that works for basically every tool.
- **Per-subprogram endpoint customization**: a service may expose more than one endpoint (ID: the iroh endpoint is the only guaranteed one today; ID may also host a website on a different standard port). Settings can declare a standard path, a homepage, or a unique-ID custom path for a subprogram; fleet uses that path raw.

## What this is

Drew, 2026-10-29: find where OpenCode-native scheduled tasks can replace the Muse cron jobs that currently launch OpenCode — to save Muse tokens or raise throughput — with proper management and monitoring of those tasks and their outcomes. Study: ~/workspace/research_notes/opencode-scheduled-tasks-20261029/findings.md.

## Verdict: PARTIAL — the trigger exists, in OpenChamber, not OpenCode

- **OpenCode core has no scheduler.** Zero cron/timer code in packages/core|server|cli; sessions are purely event-driven.
- **OpenChamber has a real scheduled-tasks subsystem** (packages/web/server/lib/scheduled-tasks/): cron/daily/weekly/once with timezones, per-project + chats scopes, new-session-per-run (model/agent pinning, permission auto-accept, goal mode with token budget, sessions stamped metadata.kind='scheduled') or prompt-into-existing-session, cross-instance occurrence claiming, loop files (.agents/loops/*.md), REST + UI + CLI + an agent tool (openchamber_schedule).
- But it is a **prompt scheduler, not a job system**: state holds only the last run, no token capture, no alerting, in-code defaults of 4 global / 2 per-project concurrent runs, and a 30-minute run cap (vs ~90-minute shift windows).

**Wave 1 (~3.4B/day of the fleet's ~5.1B/day):**
1. **Repo-queue worker shifts — ~2.26B/day, save ~2.1–2.2B.** The Muse layer is claim/checkpoint/terminal-verbs via repo-queue.py plus implem

## Gap

Drew's ruling (2026-11-03): a quota ask must terminate at the OpenCode server — not at a standalone proxy, and not at a credential store the server never sees. The Meta leg now complies: the quota gatherer (`pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/gather-quota.ts`) asks the standing fork server's `GET /api/credential` (127.0.0.1:13420) for the credential, with the direct `opencode.db` read kept only as a transport-failure fallback (the quota CLI's combined-source shape, #2490).

The **OpenDesign leg cannot comply today**, and this issue names why precisely:

1. The OpenChamber quota module's OpenDesign provider (`server/lib/quota/providers/opendesign.js` in the OpenChamber fork) does not read the OpenCode credential machinery at all. It reads a **managed session credential** from OpenChamber's own quota credential store (`~/.config/openchamber/quota/opendesign.json`): a Better Auth session cookie plus a workspace id.
2. The usage API it answers from (`https://amr-api.open-design.ai/api/auth/get-session`, `.../v1/workspaces/:id/billing/coding-plan-usage`) accepts only that session cookie (`Cookie: better-auth.session_token=…` + `x-vela-workspace-id` header). Verified live 2026-11-03: the managed cookie returns 200.
3. The credential the OpenCode server holds for integration `opendesign` is the **AMR inference API key** (`type: key`, `sk-a…`). Verified live 2026-11-03: that key is refused by the billing/session API — **403 as a Bearer token and 403 presented as the session cookie**
title: quota(opendesign): billing quota ask cannot terminate at the OpenCode server — session-cookie credential the server cannot hold or use

body:
Leg of epic #1149 (quota-plane Stage 2). Filed at Drew's direction, 2026-10-29: *"there was supposed to be a unification in the 3 quota read methods."* There wasn't — three independent quota readers exist today, they resolve credentials three different ways, and they disagree. This issue is the unification leg of #1149; it cross-links the legs it absorbs or depends on rather than replacing them.

## The three readers

1. **OpenChamber web server `/api/quota/*`** — resolves credentials through the running OpenCode server's `GET /api/credential` projection (openchamber `server/index.js:1647`; projection `server/lib/opencode/auth.js:91, 203-230`, active rows only).
2. **`openchamber quota` CLI** — server-first, with a direct credential-store fallback (`openCodeLocalCredentialSource`, reading `opencode.db` read-only). Built 2026-10-27 under #1251, which deliberately switches to the store ONLY on transport failure and stamps each row `credentialSource: server|local`.
3. **PM-stack aggregator gatherer** (`pm-stack/aggregator/scripts/gather-quota.ts:10-19, 116-149`) — reads `opencode.db` **directly, by design**, because the server-API path is known to diverge (#1251), replicates the server's projection itself, and additionally ingests bespoke per-provider file exporters (Meta: `pm-stack/meta-exporter/meta-quota-export.mjs`). Writes `quota-current.json` on a ~15-minute systemd tick.

## Divergence evidence (2026-10-29, same evening, same pools)

- **Antigravity:** the hub (reader 3)

## What

v1.1 of the OpenChamber dispatch system (design:
`files/openchamber-dispatch-babysitter-design-2026-10-26.md`): turn
the report-only babysitter into the working dispatcher + babysitter.

## Scope

- **Dispatcher:** claims queue tasks whose packet carries
  `executor: openchamber` (larger code work: effort/m+l, session-shaped
  per triage), admits against (a) location capacity and (b) the POOL
  MAP measurement gate for the routed pool (fresh quota read; ≥85% of
  window = no new heavy work). Creates the session in a per-task
  worktree on branch `queue/<task-id>-<issue>-<slug>` and records the
  binding (session id, location, pool/route, started-at) on the task.
- **Hand-back:** no slot or no headroom → park the task with reason
  class `executor-saturated` and note it on the issue. Saturation is
  reported, never a silent backlog; a Claude lane can still claim the
  task if urgent.
- **Babysitter actions:** stall nudge (one message into a session idle
  >20 min while claiming work: checkpoint/continue/state blocker; max
  2, then escalate to the monitor tracker); wall handling (quota stop =
  park blocked with the wall named, never a PAYG fallback); harvesting
  (session done → verify against GitHub → complete/park/block the task
  with labels synced and an agent-note on the issue).
- **Routing policy as config:** Fast / Workhorse (default) / Frontier

## Direction (Drew, 2026-10-28)

Reviewing the #437 decision, Drew's ruling: systemd socket activation — systemd holds the port across service restarts so connections queue instead of being refused — 'should be what we do for everything', and asked why it isn't already the pattern across the board.

## Verified current state (2026-10-28, flake at laptop ~/git/code)

Exactly ONE service does this today: OpenChamber (`systemd.user.sockets.openchamber`, `ListenStream 127.0.0.1:3000`, home/common/default.nix:999). A grep of the flake finds no other socket units, no `LISTEN_FDS` consumers, and no socket-proxyd anywhere. Everything else binds its own port and refuses connections while it restarts:

- PM stack: pm-aggregator (:4870), pm-projector (:7801) — plain systemd services.
- PM apps (Postgres, Kaneo, Grist, Pad) — Docker containers (compose today, oci-containers once #1762 lands); containers cannot inherit a systemd socket fd the same way.
- OpenCode server (laptop :13420 / tailnet serve :4096) — plain user service.
- OpenClaw gateway (:18789) — plain user service.
- cloudflared, id-mail services — to be inventoried.

## Honest constraint (why this is an audit, not a blanket flip)

Socket activation only works when the program can accept a socket handed to it by systemd (the `LISTEN_FDS` protocol — trivial shim for our own Node services, supported natively by many daemons) or when a proxy shim (systemd-socket-proxyd) in front is acceptable, which adds a hop and its own failur
title: Audit: socket activation as the default pattern for laptop services

## Design: automatic context propagation — every fleet action carries its origin

Origin: Drew, 2026-11-14. The goal: any command, session, secret lookup,
queue action, or file transfer in the fleet can be traced back to what
launched it — **automatically**, with zero per-call effort from models.
"If models have to stop and think about this every time, it has failed."

### The context record (what travels with every call)

Captured once at the outermost point available, inherited by everything
downstream:

- Muse session id + the internal model name serving it
- Queue task id + task name (when launched from the fleet queue)
- OpenCode session id + parent session id; the OpenChamber scheduled
  job that originated the session, when it came from one
- The triggering message id (internal message id of the exact message
  that led to the call) where the surface exposes it
- PID + a compact ancestor summary (enough to reconstruct the chain:
  cron → Muse → OpenCode → tool call)
- git HEAD hashes: hatch + hatch-personal repos (and the working repo
  of the call, when different)
- Host + which user-context is acting (see below)

### Mechanisms to evaluate and combine

1. **Init sourcing.** Init scripts set the environment by being
   *sourced*, not executed (`init source`), so the context variables
   persist into everything the shell launches afterward. Apply the same
   pattern on the laptop, where one OS user (`user`) is shared by
   Drew-interactive shells, OpenCode, and Claude-
title: Design: automatic context propagation — every fleet action carries its origin

❌ DO NOT journal routine

## Workstream H — Virtual filesystem over the content-addressed store

Parent program: #8983 · Proto design §H · **References, does not restate:** #9084 (content plane: addressing, GC, sensitivity tiers — the store this filesystem sits on) and #3125 (Atlas provenance/occurrence registry — in-domain prior art; the occurrence registry is this design's closest ancestor).

### The model (Drew, 2026-11-12)

- Content lands **content-addressed and immutable**: bytes are uploaded once and never change.
- **Paths are a first-class abstraction over the bytes** — a rough virtual filesystem. "Find everything referencing `geordi.png`" returns every path/location naming those bytes, across hosts and stores.
- The same bytes in five places = **one upload + five metadata records**. Each location record carries its own metadata: the path, the host it came from, the date, the process that produced/placed it — attached as metadata on the embeds/records for that location.
- Locations are editable/addable without touching the bytes: adding a sixth place that references the same content adds a metadata record, nothing else.

### Aggregated index (the performance rule)

Byte-hash and filename lookups must **not** scan the whole Atlas corpus's metadata. The virtual-file index is **aggregated**: its own Turso database, or dedicated tables maintained beside the bucket (a sidecar manifest/index uploaded alongside the content-addressed data so the bucket works standalone), with lookups by hash, by file
title: design(atlas): virtual filesystem over the content-addressed store + aggregated file index (Basin/Parquet evaluation)

Database-down resilience for coordination:

Observed 2026-11-04 ~14:05Z on the laptop with the fleet multicall binary (`repo-queue`).

`repo-queue claim --queue repo-health-code-pilot --worker repo-worker-code --lease-seconds 2700 --lane 335a5d1f-bfc1-4831-99ea-850c8939a727` exited without claiming and printed a full task-shaped JSON object whose every field was `null`. Three tasks were claimable at the time (`attempts < max_attempts`, `not_before` null, verified directly against `agent.tasks`).

Calling the broker with the same parameters claimed normally:

```
curl -s -X POST http://100.99.113.103:4801/claim -H "X-Agent-Token: ..." \
  -d '{"worker":"repo-worker-code","queue":"repo-health-code-pilot","lease_seconds":1200,"lane":"335a5d1f-bfc1-4831-99ea-850c8939a727"}'
# -> {"ok":true,"row":{"id":9341,...}}
```

So the CLI renders a null/absent row as an all-null record instead of surfacing `claim_repo_task returned no row` (a string the broker already contains) or the claimed row. A lane reading that output reasonably concludes the queue is empty and exits, wasting the run.

Expected: the claimed row, or a clear "no claimable task" error with a non-zero exit.

Found while running an OpenChamber scheduled lane; no claim was left dangling (the single claim made through the broker was parked with a resume brief on #788).

## Acceptance criteria
- `repo-queue claim` prints the claimed task's real row (id, queue, dedupe key, status) instead of an all-null row

On 2026-10-30, three NixOS switch attempts in a row died inside the mcpx derivation's checkPhase:

1. **internal/e2e burns its whole 30m timeout in the sandbox.** The suite spawns real script subprocess trees; the build sandbox has no init reaping them, so they pile up as zombies (~3,800 observed, process table degraded) and the package runs to the `go test -timeout 30m` cap: `FAIL github.com/dezren39/mcpx/internal/e2e 1800.385s`.
2. **internal/settings env tests fail in the builder environment.** `TestNoUndeclaredEnvRead` and `TestTheScriptEnvironmentIsWhatTheCodeSets` assert the process environment is exactly what the code sets; the stdenv builder env makes that untrue inside the sandbox.

Interim fix (the mechanism package.nix itself provides): both packages are in `checkExclude` in pkgs/mcpx/package.nix with the reasons recorded there. The full suite still runs in CI on main.

To restore sandbox checks:
- e2e: bound and reap spawned subprocess trees when running under a non-init supervisor, or split the process-spawning cases behind a sandbox capability check.
- settings: scope the environment assertions to the variables mcpx itself controls, ignoring builder-provided vars.

## The gap

The 2026-11-13→16 Mistral outage (57h dark) had two halves. The first half is now closed: the CDP Helium browser carrying the Mistral console session died at a laptop reboot and nothing owned it. As of 2026-11-16 it runs under a supervised systemd user unit (`helium-cdp.service`, restart-on-failure, correct profile, kill/restart recovery proven live — see #6032 comment 6910076337).

The second half is still unbuilt, and it is the half that made the outage silent for 57 hours:

1. **No stale-read detection that leads anywhere.** When a console-scraped pool's read goes stale, the quota-check stale-source escalation exists on paper (it fired once, 2026-11-14, quota-check v71) but dedupe held it forever and no repair was ever dispatched. Detection must end in a repair action, not a note.
2. **No failure classification.** On 2026-11-15 a replacement browser with the wrong profile (no Mistral session) bounced admin.mistral.ai to a login page and the gatherer reported it as `cdp-unavailable`. The design's `session-expired` class exists; the gatherer must distinguish at minimum: CDP endpoint down, browser wedged, session expired / login page, page reachable but data fetch failing.
3. **No CDP-level liveness probe.** Process supervision (`Restart=always`) catches a dead browser. A browser that is alive and still listening on :19222 but wedged (renderer hung, page unresponsive) passes supervision and fails every tick silently.

For console-scraped quota sources (M

Survey the codebase across these five areas:

- **Code Health** — confusing structure, missing or misleading error

- **Testing** — important behaviour with no coverage, tests that assert

Parent design: #8575 (one door, one home per fact — fleet tool state unification). Slice 3 of 7. Approved by Drew 2026-11-11: implement in full.

## Work

Fleet verb contract v2: every fleet queue verb declares, in the tool itself, its route order and its degraded behavior for each failure leg — GitHub write failure, GitHub read failure, database failure. The verb reports the mode it actually operated in (normal, gh-write-degraded, gh-read-degraded, db-degraded) on every call. The tool also caches a significant working set of issues from the database mirror (slice 2) so lanes spend almost no GitHub reads.

Per Drew's ruling on #8575: never stop working. No verb refuses to operate because a leg is degraded or a mirror is stale; it degrades, says so, and continues.

Lane instruction bodies then shrink to calling the verbs: all fallback improvisation comes out of the lane runbooks.

## Acceptance

- A mode line on every verb's output, machine-readable, naming the route used.
- A drill per leg: with GitHub writes blocked, claims and work proceed and outcomes buffer; with GitHub reads blocked, lanes run off the mirror and cache; with the database blocked, slice 5's replica path engages.
- Lane runbooks updated in the same change to remove local fallback logic.

Refs #12538 (tracking dispatch). Refs #12756 (mode-line slice PR for the acceptance remainder).
title: Fleet unification slice 3: fleet verb contract v2 — routes and degraded modes in the tool

## What

Implement audit disposition D-1 from #4303 (Phase 4 of #4302): when an `issues` webhook arrives with action `transferred` naming this repo as the source, delete the source-repo row via `store.deleteItem` instead of upserting it as a live item.

## Why

The Phase 4 audit (#4303) decided: **delete the source-repo row.** A `transferred` event proves the issue left the source repo; the projection contract ("a projection writes only what the event proves", #4302) means a live source-repo row renders an issue that no longer exists there. Today `applyEvent`'s issues branch falls through to `applyIssue` for `transferred`, upserting the row under the source repo.

## Blocker / first step

There is **no captured `transferred` payload anywhere in this repo**, and the payload's number semantics are unverified: whether `payload.issue.number` in the source repo's delivery is the source number or the new number decides which row key the delete targets. Deleting on an unverified key risks removing the wrong row.

The repository's GitHub App integration can list webhook delivery history but cannot read delivery payloads (`GET .../deliveries/{delivery_id}` returns 403, `Resource not accessible by integration`). Capture is therefore a hands step:

<!-- hands:v1 kind=interactive-login action="Create and transfer one throwaway issue from developing-today/code to developing-today-forks/openchamber in GitHub, then attach the raw issues/transferred delivery JSON to this issue." -->

The developing-today[bot] status automation closes GitHub issues seconds after a PR merge that merely references them (Refs-only, no closing keyword) and labels them status:done — defect tracked in #7610. A closure watchdog polling recent issue-close events in developing-today/code (plus developing-today/opencode and developing-today/openchamber, covered by the same app installation) every 15 minutes. When an automation (in practice developing-today[bot]) closes an issue and either:

then the watchdog: reopens the issue, removes the status:done label, posts a short evidence comment (closing actor, close time, closing PR, which rule fired), and reports the reopen to the ID & Atlas Space owner chat.

Relocated from dezren39/nix#377 on 2026-10-28 (placement audit): The unidentified deletion stripped git HEAD/config/loose-refs from 9 OpenCode working clones; local nix tools were already ruled out in the body and the surviving suspects are fleet/agent maintenance tooling tracked in code. Original body below; issue references inside it are historical (dezren39/nix numbering).

---

At **03:35 on 2026-10-17** something deleted `.git/HEAD`, `.git/config`, `.git/info/exclude` and all loose ref files from 9 clones under `/private/var/folders/…/T/opencode/` (argoproj, np, p, tfdd, upjet, vco, vcpx, vhct, vhct-poc). Git stopped recognising them. Objects, `packed-refs`, the index, logs and working files survived.

**Repaired:** HEAD rebuilt from `logs/HEAD` + `packed-refs` (branch where the last checkout named one, otherwise the exact last commit), plus a minimal `config` with `origin` from the clone log. All 9 work again. 7 are clean; np and p hold intentional staged deletions, now backed up (#376).

**Cause: unconfirmed.** Ruled out: `git-maintain-repos` (it only deletes `.DS_Store`) and clean.sh's sweeps (they delete whole entries, not files inside `.git`). The pattern fits macOS's daily temp cleaner, which removes files in `/private/var/folders/*/T` not *accessed* for ~3 days: the deleted files dated from the clone (Oct 13), and `description` survived because it was accessed Oct 16. But `log show` returned nothing for dirhelper, so this isn't proven.

**Why it matters:** opencod
title: Files under $TMPDIR/opencode are being deleted (9 repos lost HEAD, config and loose refs)

body:
## Finding

The nix derivation for the pkgs/id `cargo-fmt-check` flake check cannot build in a local nix sandbox: it fails while building a zig component in the check's dependency closure, before the fmt recipe ever runs.

Evidence (2026-11-14, laptop, reproduced identically on clean main `bc42ebf2` and on an unrelated fix branch — so it is not diff-caused):

```
$ cd pkgs/id && nix build .#checks.x86_64-linux.cargo-fmt-check --no-link
build.zig:4:78: error: enum 'builtin.OptimizeMode' has no member named 'small'
    const optimize = b.standardOptimizeOption(.{ .preferred_optimize_mode = .small });
note: enum declared in /nix/store/…-zig-0.16.0/lib/zig/std/builtin.zig (OptimizeMode)
```

The check's zig toolchain resolves to zig 0.16.0, whose `OptimizeMode` has no `small` member, while some `build.zig` in the closure (a dependency of the check sandbox, not pkgs/id's own code — pkgs/id has no build.zig) calls `standardOptimizeOption(.{ .preferred_optimize_mode = .small })`.

## Impact

- Any check sharing this mkCheck sandbox shape may be unbuildable locally even when its recipe is green (`cargo fmt -- --check` passes on the same tree), which hides real fmt verdicts behind a toolchain failure and pushes verification to CI runners only.
- Found during #9928's breakage verification: prettier/shellcheck/shfmt/rustfmt check derivations all build locally; cargo-fmt-check's does not, on clean main.

## Acceptance

- `nix build .#checks.x86_64-linux.cargo-fmt-check` succeeds locally
title: id: cargo-fmt-check nix derivation unbuildable locally — zig 0.16 OptimizeMode has no 'small' member in the check closure

## Problem

The PM aggregator's `/program` surface still stalls on a cold first request — the residual boot-window shape left over after #9594 was fixed. Two recurrences since lane 3c closed (PR #9861):

- **Steward run 393 — 2026-11-14 ~15:17 CST:** `/program` timed out on pass 1 (curl 000 at 25.001s, 0 bytes), then recovered on pass 2 with 200 but slow at 8.43s. (Noted on #5082: https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5082#issuecomment-6884406610)

## Background

Lane 3c (PR #9861, merged 2026-11-14 ~04:16 CST) documented the residual when it closed: in the first ~30–45s after a restart, a cold request can still 503 on empty last-good (the #9594 boot-window shape). Related closed work: #9594 (program cold start boot stall), #9781 (uncached brief comments fan out), PRs #9596 and #9835.

Tracking issue #5082 stays closed — this issue is the dedicated lane for the residual.

## Ask

Root-cause the remaining cold-path stall — the empty last-good window and/or the slow first build — so a cold `/program` request never 503s or times out: the first request after a restart should serve last-good or a fast build, not fail.

You are "Bolt" ⚡ - a performance-obsessed agent who makes the codebase faster, one optimization at a time.

✅ **Always do:**
- Run commands like `pnpm lint` and `pnpm test` (or associated equivalents) before creating PR

- Measure and document expected performance impact

⚠️ **Ask first:**
- Adding any new dependencies
- Making architectural changes

🚫 **Never do:**
- Modify package.json or tsconfig.json without instruction
- Make breaking changes

- Sacrifice code readability for micro-optimizations

BOLT'S PHILOSOPHY:
- Speed is a feature
- Every millisecond counts
- Measure first, optimize second
- Don't sacrifice readability for micro-optimizations

- A performance bottleneck specific to this codebase's architecture

Parent: #2050 (investigation: BitTorrent-style chunk retrieval for graph objects), epic #2056. Follow-up B of the #2050 investigation. Depends on the holder-discovery follow-up A (provider table) — a hand-fed provider list is acceptable for the PoC's benchmarks.

## Problem
Retrieval in `pkgs/id` is single-source: `src/commands/get.rs` does one `store.remote().fetch(conn, hash)` over one connection. iroh-blobs (0.103, in Cargo.toml) already supports the swarm-shaped pieces — `(hash, ChunkRanges)` requests per provider, bao verified streaming (each 16 KiB chunk group verified against the blob's BLAKE3 root hash as it arrives, from any source, in any order), partial-blob state in FsStore, and providers reporting the exact missing location when they close a stream for data they lack. What does not exist is the scheduling policy that uses several holders at once.

## Scope — PROOF OF CONCEPT (review-gated; do not build the permanent feature on it)
Implement the #2050 §5 retrieval flow as a PoC in the `get` path:
- Wanted-set = chunk-group ranges of the hash; assign ranges rarest-first across the provider set; disjoint ranges per holder; start with ≤4 concurrent sources.
- Verified groups persist to FsStore immediately (resume + become servable partial state). Bad group → discard, requeue range, deprioritise that holder for the hash. Missing-range stream close → shrink that holder's ranges, requeue elsewhere.
- Endgame: duplicate-request trailing in-flight ranges; first verified c

Five-word summary: configure rotation without code changes.

Follow-on to #8887 (closed; the passthrough itself works and is proven live). Everything below is about the rotation's CONFIGURATION surface, verified from the source (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet/src/gh.rs`, main @ 2026-11-14) plus live probes on 2026-11-14.

## Where it stands today (facts, not asks)

- The three Apps are a compiled-in enum (`GhApp::{Fleet, DevToday, Backup}`, `GhApp::ALL`); each App's private-key secret name is a code constant, and two of the three App IDs also come from broker secrets (`kaneo.github-app-id`, `github-app.backup-app-id`). Adding a fourth App today requires a code change + redeploy.
- Order and owner sets are env-only: `FLEET_GH_ORDER` replaces the whole rotation for one process; `FLEET_GH_APP_OWNERS` / `FLEET_GH_DEVTODAY_OWNERS` / `FLEET_GH_BACKUP_OWNERS` replace per-App owner lists. Nothing persists between shells/machines.
- Default owner lists are compiled in and small: fleet App — developing-today, developing-today-forks, dezren39; developing.today App — developing-today, dezren39; backup App — developing-today only. **Symptom.** When a needs-drew question (code#8568) is answered, its alert incident stays `open` forever. The aggregator has no close path for `needs-drew:<ledgerId>` incidents: the answer endpoint records the answer, the candidate disappears (no re-push), but the incident row is never closed, so the board accumulates answered questions as open incidents.

**Evidence.** The #8568 live proof run, 2026-11-11: question `proof-8568-needs-drew` raised 07:44:12Z, push sent 07:44:12.982Z, answer recorded 07:44:35Z (`optionId: seen, via: api`), task 14917 unblocked + cancelled — the incident was still `open` minutes later and was closed by hand through the aggregator's own Supabase client (`status='closed', closed_at=now()`; verified in `/api/alerts.json`).

**Scope.** In the aggregator's answer path (where `recordAnswer` succeeds for a needs-drew question), close the open incident for key `needs-drew:<ledgerId>` — the store already has `AlertsStore.closeOpenIncidentByKey` (built for stack-health "up" events in #8568). Same treatment when a raised question's task is cancelled without an answer, if a clean signal for that exists; otherwise answer-close alone is the fix.

**Acceptance.** Raise a test needs-drew question, answer it, and read back the incident as `closed` in `/api/alerts.json` with no manual store write. No change to push behavior (answered questions already stop re-pushing).

Refs: #8568 (Phase 1), design `pm-stack-notifications-design-2026-11-11.md` §5/§8.

## From the #2059 investigation (hot-world sharding)

The landed investigation doc for #2059 (`doc/2026-10-30T19-35-00Z_investigation_hot_world_sharding/`, §3 rung 3) designs native-node spill for an indivisible hot world: a native `id` node runs the world's program turns while the hosted Durable Object keeps the journal of record. The doc is explicit that **the journaled single-writer lease is the whole safety design** — split-brain (DO and native node both accepting writes) is the catastrophic failure. The lease protocol itself was not designed. This issue designs it, so the #2046 synthesis adopts a designed protocol instead of a placeholder.

## Design to produce

- **Lease object**: grant/revoke/handoff as journaled entries — who grants (DO? coordinator? operator?), lease term and renewal, and how the grant is recorded so both sides and any auditor can prove who held the write lease at any journal position.
- **Fencing**: how a partitioned or crashed ex-holder is fenced out (monotonic lease epoch checked on journal append is the obvious shape — verify or replace), and what happens to writes an ex-holder attempts after losing the lease.
- **Handoff both ways**: DO → native at spill start, native → DO at de-escalation (investigation §2: spill ends when the warning band clears for ~1 hour), including in-flight command treatment at the boundary.
- **Failure walkthroughs**: native node crashes holding the lease; DO and node partitioned while both alive; lease expires mid-turn;
title: id: design: native-spill write lease protocol for hot worlds (from #2059)

body:
Follow-up from the key-recovery investigation on #2060 (doc: `investigations/key-recovery.md` in the ID program workspace, §1/§3/§7). Parent epic: #2056.

## Problem
`pkgs/id` identity is a single Iroh Ed25519 secret key (`src/local.rs`: `SecretKey::generate()` / `open_with_key`); the public key IS the account (invites name it directly, `src/invite.rs`). There is no indirection for device keys, revocation, IdP bindings, or rotations — so a lost key is a lost identity and a second device is a second account.

## Proposal
Design (then implement) a signed keyset/authorization log as the identity substrate: an identity identifier plus an append-only chain of signed records — device-key enrolment/revocation, hosted IdP claim bindings (#2044 §4.3 option 1), guardian sets (see social-recovery follow-up), and key rotations. Group membership and directory records bind to the identity, not to one key. Keyset-admin operations (add/revoke device, change guardians) are narrower-scoped than everyday signing.

## Acceptance
- [ ] Design doc section or ADR covering record formats, fold/verification rules, and the identity identifier derivation.
- [ ] Enrolment + revocation of a second device key via QR/invite-style pairing (`src/qr.rs`, `src/invite.rs` surfaces exist).
- [ ] Existing group-encryption per-device sessions (`src/encryption/`) consume device keys from the keyset.
- [ ] Old single-key accounts migrate via a genesis keyset record signed by the existing key.
title: id: keyset/authorization log — device keys, revocation, bindings as signed records (identity substrate)

Work is steadily moving off the main agent onto other systems that spend their own tokens under direction — the OpenCode fleet, OpenClaw-originated sessions, Codex/ChatGPT, Jules and other external agents. ## Incident (2026-10-28, laptop amd-6)

The laptop was unreachable fleet-wide ~06:11–09:00 CDT. Journal evidence:

- `06:12:29 systemd-logind: hybrid-sleep requested from client PID 38231 ('upowerd') ... The system will hybrid sleep now!`
- `06:12:29 systemd[1]: Reached target Sleep` / `systemd-sleep: Performing sleep operation 'hybrid-sleep'` / kernel `PM: hibernation: hibernation entry`
- `08:53:10 systemd[1]: Stopped target Sleep` (resume)

UPower's critical-power action (`CriticalPowerAction=HybridSleep`, PercentageAction=2, PercentageCritical=5, TimeAction=120) fired on a reading that could not have been real: no low-battery warnings were logged beforehand, and minutes after resume the battery read **99%, Charging, AC online=1**. A real drain to 2% cannot recharge to 99% that fast. Most likely a glitched time-to-empty/percentage sample (the machine also carries several churning UCSI USB-C power-source entries). Cost: a ~2h40m fleet-wide laptop outage (46 queue items parked on the outage tracker).

UPower has no "wait and re-check" setting — it acts on a single sample. Drew's direction: keep sleep as the response to a *genuine* critical battery (this machine is normally on AC, but if it were on battery, sleep beats a hard power loss); a false sleep is worse than either.

## The guard (built + tested 2026-10-28)

A small poller that adds the missing confirmation step. Tested implementation already exists on the laptop at `~/tools/power-guard.py` (python3, no deps):

- Poll

Survey the codebase across these five areas:

- **Security** — unsafe input handling, secrets or credentials in code or

- **Code Health** — confusing structure, missing or misleading error

Pool changes proposed by pool-intelligence flags or the steward's

- A test is a small batch of comparable real tasks (same kind/effort
  class, drawn from the live queues) run on the candidate

  Minimum viable batch: 3 tasks per arm for a directional read, 6 for

  input + output), stalls/nudges, rework within 48h (follow-up fixes

  failed one retires the flag with its numbers attached.

Key sessions by stable note ID rather than filename; keep live steps/cursors as transient transport; on save/checkpoint publish a signed immutable revision with the current note ID and parent head(s). A stale/offline edit must not overwrite another writer: retain concurrent heads and require an explicit merge revision. Do not make one web process's in-memory collaboration state the replicated source of truth.

Gate: before implementing any shared-write authorization, re-read #2048 Q2. Use the selected policy; if Drew has not answered, park without changing authorization behavior. - Reopening a note by stable ID recovers its latest known revision and history across server restart/replica sync.
- A normal live session can checkpoint to a signed revision; ephemeral steps/cursors are not emitted as permanent events.
- Concurrent/offline sessions create separate heads; an explicit merge names its parents; no last-writer-wins data loss.

Exploration opened by Drew 2026-11-04, after the Snowflake swap landed. Three threads, in the order they should be evaluated:

## 1. Parallel branch execution (near-term, small)
A hybrid query has independent branches (FTS branch, vector branch, plus filters) that only join at RRF fusion. Today they run effectively serially in the Python CLI. Follow-up to #8777 (the 2026-11-11T22:01:09Z SIGTERM that killed pm-aggregator and pm-dispatch in the same second, sender unidentified).

## Why

The laptop kernel supports auditing (CONFIG_AUDIT=y, CONFIG_AUDITSYSCALL=y) but no audit tooling is installed and no rules exist, so a signal sent by hand leaves no record anywhere: systemd logs the death, never the sender. The two pm units are covered meanwhile by the sigterm-witness wrapper (live via drop-ins; declarative in PR #8786), but every other process on the box is still unattributed.

## Ask

Enable auditd declaratively in the laptop's NixOS configuration, with rules that log signal-sending syscalls with the sender's identity, e.g.:

```
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S kill -S tkill -S tgkill -k signal-attribution
```

so any future "who killed this process" question is answered by `ausearch -k signal-attribution` (auid, exe, pid, comm of the sender) instead of an investigation.

## Notes / constraints

- This needs root and a system activation — it cannot be hot-installed. Ride the coordinated switch or a maintenance window; do not hand-install packages outside the NixOS config.
- Signal syscalls are not a hot path on this box; expected log volume is low. Keep the rule set to kill-family syscalls only.
- The witness on the pm units stays: it is per-service, survives even if auditd is later dropped, and its log sits next to the service's state.

## Acceptance

From a marked shell, send SIGTERM to a throwaway process; show t
title: Attribution: declarative auditd for signal syscalls on the laptop (follow-up to #8777)

The quota-recorder systemd units (`quota-recorder.service` / `quota-recorder.timer`, installed as imperative copies in `/etc/systemd/system`) still vanish mid-boot and stay gone until a person or a sweep notices and hand-reinstalls them. Recording silently stops in the gap.

## Evidence
- #6148 (closed 2026-11-05 as COMPLETED) fixed the filed defect: a restore block in `~/tools/init.sh` plus `~/tools/quota-recorder/install.sh` (dezren39/hatch `3efce1255`). Verified 2026-11-17 audit: `init.sh` contains the restore block and the timer is currently active.
- But the restore only runs at init/boot. On 2026-11-16 the units were lost at least 3 times in ~14 hours (fleet run reports, `~/memory/2026-11-16.md`), including one sweep recording verbatim: "quota-recorder units had vanished from /etc again — reinstalled via ~/tools/quota-recorder/install.sh; timer active, tick landed". Each loss was healed by a manual reinstall, not by the #6148 mechanism.
- Working pattern: imperative `/etc` unit copies are wiped by NixOS switch activations mid-boot; nothing re-runs the installer until the next boot or a human notice.

## Scope
Give the quota-recorder units a restore path that fires mid-boot — e.g. declare the units in the Nix configuration so switch activations carry them, or add a switch/post-activation hook (or a watchdog timer in a durable unit family) that re-runs `~/tools/quota-recorder/install.sh` when the timer is missing. Sandbox side (the recorder runs on the sandbox)
title: quota-recorder: units still vanish mid-boot — #6148 restore block only heals at init, switch activations wipe the /etc copies with no mid-boot restore

## Finding (R2 review, 2026-11-01)

The Supabase backup staging uploads (`supabase-backups` bucket, `pg/muse-dev/staging/` prefix, written by `supabase_backup.py` from the laptop) leak **incomplete multipart uploads** when an upload fails or is interrupted: the staging object is retried under a new key and the failed upload is never aborted.

Evidence: 6 orphaned multipart uploads found initiated 2026-10-26 → 2026-10-30 (2 with one 8 MiB part each uploaded, 4 with no parts — 16 MiB of stored parts total). All 6 were aborted during the 2026-11-01 review and the bucket verified back to 0 incomplete uploads. Separately, one *completed* staging object (`pg/muse-dev/staging/f4b085ed-….api.jsonl.zst`, 10.8 MB, 2026-10-27) was left behind in staging. It is **not** accounted for: its sha256 (`5d38249d…`, computed during the review) appears neither in `pg/muse-dev/manifest.json` nor as a final hash-named object, so it may be the only copy of that export — the review left it untouched. Staging is neither cleaned nor reconciled after a run.

The byte cost today is trivial; the defect is that failed runs accumulate invisible state in the bucket (multipart parts don't show in normal object listings) and the staging prefix silently diverges from "empty between runs".

## Ask

- In `supabase_backup.py`: abort the multipart upload on any failure path (S3 `AbortMultipartUpload`); on success, finalize the staging object (hash-name + manifest entry) or remove it — and reconcile the one already

Extends #5741 (SPLADE investigation + eval harness + adaptive weighting). Design commitments from Drew's direction 2026-11-04.

## What this adds

Two NEW front-end stages in front of retrieval, each independently toggleable (**off / deprioritized / on**), in pipeline order:

**spell correction → query planner/rewriter → signal weighting (#5741) → fan-out**

## Stage 1 — spell correction

Neither BM25 nor SPLADE tolerates typos: both match on exact terms. The mechanism is classical, not learned:

- **Candidate generation** by Damerau–Levenshtein edit distance (a transposition — flipped letters — counts as 1 edit) plus **character-trigram similarity** (set overlap over character 3-grams; the Jaccard family already in the stack per #5733).
- Candidates are drawn from a **corpus-vocabulary dictionary with term frequencies**, so corrections prefer terms the corpus actually contains.
- Correction is **conservative — high-confidence only**. The original query is **always retained as a variant**; a correction is never silently substituted. The raw and corrected forms can both fan out and merge like any other variant (see dual submission below).

## Stage 2 — query planner / rewriter

A small, fast model rephrases/expands the query into a retrieval-shaped variant: vocabulary the corpus would use, expansions of abbreviations, decomposed compound questions.

- **Dual submission is the default shape**: raw and rewritten both fan out; results merge with **provenance tags** (`raw-only` /
title: atlas search: query-understanding front-end — spell correction + LLM query planner/rewriter as toggleable stages, dual submission with provenance (extends #5741)

## Summary

The collab server accepts, stores, broadcasts and Acks `ProseMirror` steps without ever checking that they parse or apply — one invalid step poisons a document session for every current and future client.

In `pkgs/id/src/web/collab.rs` a step is an opaque blob end to end:

- `Step` is a flattened `serde_json::Value` (`collab.rs:164-169`) — there is no parse or validation constructor.
- `CollabMessage::decode` (`collab.rs:536-545`) accepts a Steps frame as `(u8, u64, Vec<serde_json::Value>, u64)`: any JSON values at all count as "steps".
- The Steps handler (`collab.rs:986-1052`) checks only that the frame's version equals the current version, then pushes every step into `doc.steps` (:1019-1024), bumps the version by `steps.len()` (:1028), broadcasts an `Update` to the other clients (:1032-1036) and Acks the sender (:1044-1052). It never applies the steps to a document and never asks whether they are well-formed.
- On join, the catch-up path (`collab.rs:787-810`) replays **all** stored steps to the new client, so a stored bad step is re-delivered forever, for the life of the `Document` (cleanup only runs an hour after the last client disconnects).

Auth is not a gate: a client that sends no AUTH frame in 5 seconds "proceeds as anonymous" (`collab.rs:694-755`) and can send Steps. A merely buggy or version-skewed client reaches the same place without malice — e.g. a step built against a diverged local doc, or a node type an older/newer web build's schema does not sh
title: id(web): collab server stores and broadcasts steps it never validates — one bad step poisons the document's history and loops every client

Follow-up from the #2065 design (`doc/2026-10-29T12-10-00Z_design_refundable_grants_pending_transfers/`, PR #2293), §6.3.

## Why

The pending-transfer mechanism adds failure modes the posted design did not have: a service that dies between reserve and vest leaves the user's paid grant to expire on the TigerBeetle `timeout`, and a crash between writing intent and submitting the transfer leaves a row whose state disagrees with the ledger.

## Scope

- Sweeper: `state=pending AND window_ends_at < now` → post (retry with backoff), then mark `posted`; `Expired` is a reconcilable state, not a loss.
- Safety net: `timeout` = window + slack (design recommends +72h) so a dead service cannot hold a grant forever; the sweeper must post before that, and the slack is a last resort.
- Drift alarm: compare each grant's `pending_transfer_id` resolution in TigerBeetle against the row state; mismatch is an alert (never a silent fix).
- Late-refund fallback per §6.2: clawback attempt, on `exceeds_credits` mark the grant `debt` and expose it to the gateway's grant/redemption refusal.
- Metrics: pending count, oldest pending age, expired-then-reconciled count, drift count, debt total.

## Depends on

The grant service issue (creates the table and endpoints this reads).

## Done when

A test cluster with a killed service between reserve and vest self-heals via the sweeper, a seeded drift row raises an alarm, and an after-vest refund lands in `debt` rather than throwing.

Part of epic #1184 (PM stack coherence — wave 2, 2026-10-26).

The stack's sources disagree regularly — Project Status vs the aggregator's derived state, Kaneo card state vs GitHub issue state — and today each disagreement lives where it happens to render: a ⚠ badge on /projects, invisible everywhere else, with no way to resolve the class of problem, only the instance. A source-conflict inbox collects every live disagreement into one queue: each entry names the item, the two sources, both values, and how long they have disagreed. Drew (or the orchestrator, for classes Drew has ruled on) records a per-class ruling — "for Kaneo-vs-GitHub state, trust GitHub" — and the ruling applies to that class going forward, recorded as data (not code), until changed. Resolved classes stop generating inbox entries; a source that starts disagreeing in a new way creates a new class rather than re-opening an old ruling silently.

Acceptance:
- One page lists all current source disagreements across facets (not only /projects), each with item, sources, both values, and disagreement age.
- A per-class "trust source X" ruling can be recorded, is stored as data, and measurably suppresses that class's entries while applying the trusted value in renders.
- Rulings are listed and revocable in the same place; revoking re-surfaces the class's current disagreements.
- The inbox count appears in the stack health surface so a growing conflict backlog is itself visible; covered by tests with seeded disagreem
title: feat(aggregator): source-conflict inbox — one resolvable queue for Project-vs-derived and Kaneo-vs-GitHub disagreements, with per-class trust rulings

## Problem (five words: silent mode deletion shadows claimant)

The opencode claimant's mode file (`~/.local/state/opencode-claimant/mode` on the laptop) is an unguarded single point of failure: when the file is missing, the claimant silently defaults to shadow mode (discovery only, no launches) with no signal. This has now bitten twice:

- 2026-11-08: mode file missing, claimant never launched anything until set to `live` by hand.
- 2026-11-14: `fires.jsonl` shows reads flipping live -> shadow at 14:46Z; the file was deleted ~5.5h after working live fires (deleter unattributed from available logs). This blocked the #9106 summit dispatch (`mode_not_live`, task 15354) until restored under Drew's authorization.

## Acceptance

- Mode file deletion or unreadability produces a VISIBLE alert within one surfacing cycle (wire into the #10141 silent-failure surfacing, now live) instead of a silent shadow fallback.
- Claimant startup/heartbeat records the mode it read and where from, so a flip is attributable in the log after the fact.
- Consider making the mode part of managed config (repo/systemd state) rather than a bare file any process can delete.
- A missing file must never again present as 'summits just aren't launching' for hours.

Refs: #9106, #10141, #9103. Filed from the 2026-11-14 summit-pool investigation (Track B).
title: claimant mode file: guard the silent-deletion single point of failure

The Phase 4 audit (#5763) fixed the same-shape sites in-phase (invented substitute directories: root anchoring, CWD fallback, literal `~`, hardcoded `/home/user`). The `os.homedir()` surface is a genuinely different shape:

# DR verdict — whole PM-stack backup audit, 2026-11-14

Ordered by Drew 2026-11-14: *"Are there any other obvious gaps to our backup routines? Is the rest of the PM stack backed up? If I start up a brand-new computer, could we use backups to get the entire PM stack running?"*

Method: read-only audit. Implements the policy + federation layers of the owner decision on #185 (comment 6486250456, Drew, 2026-10-28). Likely splits into smaller issues; filed whole so the design stays in one place. Depends on the marker + default-view work (tag.clear as a role-aware marker).

## Pieces
1. **Delete requests.** A first-class operation: anyone can request deletion of a tag, carrying a reason. The request is delivered to the relevant authority holders — the tag's author, group admins, or server owners — and their grant/decline is recorded.
2. **Server delete policies.** A server admin can set policies on their own server that actually delete based on clear markers (and/or granted delete requests). Conditions are the server's business; nothing here is protocol-mandated. Deletes are events (auditable), not silent state edits.
3. **Federated deletes (opt-in per server owner, never default).**
   - A server owner may replicate deletes from federated co-servers.
   - A server owner may accept delete events from ANY server provided the delete is signed by the author or admins and the full chain validates; an invalid or incomplete chain means the foreign delete is not honored.

## Acceptance
- Delete request round-trips: request with reason -> delivered to author/admins/server owners -> grant produces a delete under the server's policy, decline is recorded with no delete.
- A server with no delete policy never hard-deletes from clear markers alone.

Extends #5741 (SPLADE investigation + eval harness) and #5668 (query-embed cache + flags). Design commitments from Drew's direction 2026-11-04.

## Principle

**Anything not baked into how data is stored must be settable per query** — from the fleet-binary CLI flags AND from the raw query format (the full-access path), with **identical parameter names** in both — so values can be benchmarked and better defaults found **without editing code**.

If a retrieval constant lives in code today, that's a bug against this principle.

## Knob inventory (v1, extensible)

- **Per-shard top-k** — how many results each shard returns into the fan-out.
- **Global fan-in top-k** — how many combined results survive the merge.
- **Per-signal weights** — dense, BM25, SPLADE (the #5741 adaptive-weighting defaults, overridable per query).
- **Per-signal multipliers** — score scaling per signal, distinct from the weights.
- **Jaccard rescore depth** — candidate count entering the #5733 rescore stage.
- **Jaccard boost threshold** — the overlap at which the rescore boost applies.
- **RRF constant k** — if reciprocal-rank fusion is used in the merge, its k is a knob, never a hardcoded 0.6.
- **Stage toggles** — planner and spell correction off / deprioritized / on (companion issue: query-understanding front-end, extends #5741).
- **Hint override** — force the query class (code / docs / error / concept) instead of the classifier's call.
- **Variant selection** — raw / rewritten / both.
- **Expand-N**

## Evidence

`pkgs/id/src/serve_proxy.rs:52-56` defines finite initial stream and connection credits, but `CreditWindow::grant` at lines 415-418 uses `saturating_add` with no upper bound or error result. Each decoded `WINDOW_UPDATE` can grant a `u32` amount (`window_update_amount`, lines 234-247); repeated valid updates can therefore grow available credit arbitrarily up to `u64::MAX`. Once the mux uses this primitive, the sender can be authorized to exceed the receiver's bounded in-flight buffers. Saturation only hides integer overflow; it does not enforce a finite credit ceiling.

The relay backpressure design explicitly requires hard finite per-stream and aggregate per-connection byte limits, and says credit returns only as bounded buffer space is released (`doc/2026-11-08T11-08-53Z_design_id5813_relay_proxy_protocol/2026-11-08T11-08-53Z_design_id5813_relay_proxy_protocol.md:85-100`). The serve-proxy issue #7569 is closed and #5792 remains the protocol design tracker, but neither specifically tracks a maximum-credit guard. All-state searches for `CreditWindow`, `WINDOW_UPDATE`, and bounded flow control found no matching implementation issue. The currently open #8951 concerns frame stream/sequence semantics, not credit accounting; no open PR implements this guard.

## Why it matters

A peer can repeatedly send valid credit updates and defeat the flow-control bound that is supposed to keep per-stream and per-connection buffering finite. This risks unbounded queued/in-flight d

## Summary

mcpx reads responses from endpoints it does not control — third-party MCP servers, configured model providers, remote embeddings services — with no byte bound in four places. A client timeout bounds *duration*, never *bytes*: a fast endpoint can deliver gigabytes inside the timeout. Each filing re-derived the same missing rule in a different package:

- **Daemon chat-completions proxy** — `proxyToUpstream` (`internal/daemon/routes_proxy.go:244`) uses `http.DefaultClient` (no deadline at all) and streams the response through a `TeeReader` into an unbounded `bytes.Buffer` kept as the feedback record (#2114; implementation PR #3380 in flight).

- **Both OpenAI-compatible providers** — `internal/model/openai.go:123` and `internal/scripting/provider.go:121` buffer whole; on non-2xx the entire body is embedded in the error (#4354; probe: a 32 MiB error body produced a 33.5 MB error string). The `baseURL` is configuration (OpenAI, a company gateway, LiteLLM, Ollama, LM Studio).

**Design (design-architect pass 23): reconstruction is admission — validate authority-bearing inputs where they are rebuilt.**

Design doc: `files/designs/code-id-reconstruction-validation.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace. Audited against origin/main `206f4fd7`.

## Summary

Six issues filed independently in one evening are one defect with six addresses: in `pkgs/id`, data that carries authority is validated when it is created live, and trusted when it is reconstructed — a world journal being restored, an attestation being computed from decoded objects, a manifest being parsed, a schedule cap being checked. The live path enforces invariants (only issued, JOIN-holding participants act; claims answer the agreement they name; a manifest step means what it says); the reconstruction paths enforce almost none of them, so a crafted or corrupted artefact acquires authority the live path would never have granted.

**The recorded rule:** reconstruction is admission. Anywhere `pkgs/id` rebuilds authority-bearing state from stored or supplied data, the rebuilding code validates the same invariants the live path enforces at creation, and refuses (never partially applies, never silently repairs) data that violates them. Corollaries: validate against state you hold, not claims the input makes; unnamed means refused (scope bits, manifest keys, outcomes); the system shape (sequence 0 / participant 0) is not borrowable by authority-carrying entries.

# PM stack: close authority — automation must never close an issue

Program epic from Drew's 2026-11-14 order: "review this entire system end to end and make the best fix possible… make something coherent that doesn't break this way."

## Why this exists

Defect #7610 (CLOSED): Kaneo's GitHub integration closed issues seconds after Refs-only PR merges. Root causes were structural, not a single bad setting:

1. **Close authority was never assigned.** GitHub issue state, `status:*` labels, Kaneo columns, and queue rows are all mirrored state with multiple writers. Parent: #2050 (investigation: BitTorrent-style chunk retrieval for graph objects), epic #2056. Follow-up C of the #2050 investigation. Depends on follow-up A (holder discovery + wired blob gate).

## Problem
In the #2050 design every downloader becomes a useful partial holder the moment its first chunk group verifies — FsStore persists verified ranges, and bao verification makes a partial holder's ranges exactly as trustworthy as a complete holder's. Nothing in `pkgs/id` enables, announces, or budgets that re-serving today, and turning it on widens the serving surface: swarm range-serving must be covered by the LIST 8 abuse controls (per-IP / per-ID / per-world MB and message budgets, rate limits) before any public server serves swarm traffic.

## Scope
- A node serving a world re-serves the verified ranges it holds for that world's blobs, subject to the blob gate (members of a referencing world only).
- Announce partial holdings through follow-up A's provider table/announcements (held-ranges summary, not just complete/partial boolean).
- Wire serving budgets: per-world and per-peer caps on swarm range-serving (bytes/window), reusing the LIST 8 budget shapes; a node over budget declines new range requests cleanly (requester requeues elsewhere — the #2050 flow already tolerates this).
- Eviction policy: LRU under store pressure for fetched blobs; a node configured as a world's public server must not silently evict that world's only-known copy — surface it in config/status inst

## Problem

Every fleet lane authenticates as one account, so GitHub's content-creation ceiling (documented: ~80/min, 500/hour) is a single shared budget no job can see. On 2026-10-28 `developing-today/code` alone produced 2 916 content-creating events (479 issues/PRs + 2 437 comments), peaking at 511 in the 22:00Z hour; creation then stopped for 31m48s after #1999. `gh issue create` exited 0 with empty output while creating nothing, so no caller noticed.

## Scope

Code lands with the fleet tooling (`~/hatch/tools`, `repo-queue.py`, producer/filing scripts), not in this repository. This issue is the tracking record and the spec pointer.

1. **Creation ledger** — `~/.local/state/fleet/content-ledger.sqlite`, one row per content-creating call (`ts_utc, actor, job, repo, kind, ref, outcome`), written as a reservation before the call and finalised after the verifying read; windows computed from the ledger (60 s, 3 600 s), atomic across processes via `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`.
2. **Throttle wrapper** — `reserve(job, kind)` before every create. Account-wide 45/min and 300/hour; ≥ 1 s between POSTs; ≤ 8 in flight; per-lane 50/hour sustained with idle share reclaimable; 75/hour reserve for priority-10 breakage work; bulk programs ≤ 20 issues per 30-m

**Design scope only — no data moves in this issue's first pass.**

## What moves
- From: Supabase (`muse-dev2`) `ci.events` (10,952 live rows, 31.8 MB — ~2.9 KB/row of jsonb webhook payload)
- To: Turso, staging tier, partitioned by day/repo

## Why
A pure append-only CI webhook ledger: 10,957 inserts / 0 updates in the stats window since 2026-10-29, no foreign keys, read by scan (its one view, `ci.recent_failures`, is a filtered scan). It is the fastest-growing table in the project by bytes and has no transactional consumer — under the §9 placement rule it is a Turso stream, not Postgres state.

Design doc: §9 of `doc/2026-11-04T21-27-34Z_design_atlas_scaler_revision/` (PR #5667, addendum PR #5689).

## Risks
- The webhook receiver is a live write path — cutover must not drop events during deploys (receiver-side buffering or dual-write).
- `recent_failures` consumers (alerting? dashboards?) must be inventoried first; failure-visibility must not regress during the move.
- Retention is currently unbounded; the Turso design should state a retention window rather than replicating unbounded growth.

## Sketch of steps
1. Inventory the receiver(s) and every reader of `ci.events` / `ci.recent_failures`.
2. Design the Turso table + a `recent_failures`-equivalent query; set retention (propose 90 days hot, cold export beyond).
3. Dual-write at the receiver, backfill the retention window, diff failure queries.
4. Flip readers, stop the Postgres write, keep the Postgres table read-only
title: design: move ci.events webhook ledger from Supabase to Turso staging

Part of epic #1184; implementation follow-up of design issue #1259 (spend rollups). Design note: `doc/spend-rollups-design-1259.md`. Depends on the rollup-store slice of #1259.

## Scope
Detect cost anomalies from the spend rollups and surface them through the existing alert throat (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/alerts.ts`, #3676) into Needs-you (/attention) and the Today/brief summary — no new notification path.

## Anomaly classes (v1, thresholds are named constants with tests, per the design note)
- **Burn without progress:** an epic/project consumes spend in a window while closing zero child issues in the same window.
- **Single-session dominance:** one root session accounts for more than the threshold share of an epic's window spend.
- **Unattributed growth:** the unattributed share of total spend rises window-over-window beyond the threshold.
- **Charge without activity:** a matched PAYG charge for a service with no corresponding session/quota activity in its period.

## Rules
- Missing or partial data suppresses the anomaly, never fabricates it: an anomaly needs a complete window on both sides of its comparison.
- Each surfaced anomaly names its evidence: scope, window, the two compared values, and a link to the rollup/drill-down.
- Delivery class: page + ledger (warning) in v1; no push, per the alerts design (warnings never push in v1).

## Acceptance criteria
- One test per anomaly class: fires on the constructed pattern, silent on partial data, silent just below threshol
title: impl(pm-stack): cost-anomaly detection to Needs-you via the alert throat (#1259 slice 4)

# Design mill pass 2: iroh-native ID transport in fleet — identity, postcards, format conversion

Part of the fleet-surface design mill (Drew, 2026-11-14). Parent issue cross-links all passes.

## What to design

ID's native transport is iroh, which needs full iroh credentials and protocols — the one tool the plain pass-through of pass 1 cannot cover. Two levels:

### Level 1: raw proxy
Fleet proxies raw input/output over an iroh connection without handling the payload. Also design the relay-aware variant: a proxy that uses iroh itself to do the transfer (not mere packet forwarding) while still requiring something on the far end that speaks the protocol.

### Level 2: fleet as iroh initiator
Fleet fully handles the iroh connection and is the initiator:

- **Credentials**: fleet handles the iroh credentials, or the caller provides a secret key. Default: fleet generates a random key per session as part of its ID stamp; the public key is attached to queue items it picks up and everywhere else the stamp goes, and stored in an environment variable when the stamp is dot-sourced. (This extends the context-propagation design in code#10357.)
- **Byte streaming**: stream bytes from the caller in, and bytes back out on stdout/stderr-style streams.
- **Postcard-native mode**: fleet targets the ID postcard shape and sends/receives postcard values directly — postcards in and out, one at a time, or wrapped for wire e
title: Design mill pass 2: iroh-native ID transport in fleet — identity, postcards, format conversion

## What this is

#alignment (C0CBYQR65LL) is the agent coordination channel. Aster is in it and proposed the channel contract on 2026-10-28 (verified senders; every dispatch carries ID/owner/scope/evidence; ACK/BLOCKED then RESULT in-thread; dedupe; no credentials). OpenClaw is not in it yet — its bot binding and delivery are unverified. Drew asked 2026-10-29 to add OpenClaw and to settle whether one channel for all agents is enough, or each pair needs its own point-to-point path.

## The topology question

**One shared channel** (recommended):
- Channels stay O(1) as agents are added; pairwise grows O(n^2).
- Every dispatch and result sits in one record — the OpenClaw/OpenCode review needs to see traffic it was not part of.
- Threads per dispatch keep it readable; the contract keeps it disciplined.

**Point-to-point per pair**:
- Wins only for high-volume pair traffic, or content that should not be visible to the other agents.

## Summary

Implement spill v2 phase 3 from the #5787 design (`doc/2026-11-08_design_id5787.md`, §4): multi-world spill on one host — admission control and resource fairness between spilled worlds.

## Scope

- Per-world budgets on a spill host: turn CPU time, concurrent in-flight turns, append submission rate, replay bandwidth. A world over budget is throttled at its own executor; heat alone never revokes a lease.
- Control-traffic priority: renewal submissions and replay catch-up for other worlds schedule ahead of a hot world's mutation submissions, so one world's flood cannot false-expire a neighbour.
- Grant-time admission control: the DO's selection policy treats a host at its holder budget as ineligible; an unplaceable spill waits as pending intent instead of over-committing the host.

## Trigger / gating

**Do not start until trigger T3 fires:** the first host holding (or asked to hold) more than one spilled world, or a #5685 fairness case is run against a spill host. Design: #5787. Composes with: #5685. Depends on: #3805.

## Acceptance

- [ ] The design §7 two-worlds-one-floods case passes: the flooding world is throttled at its budget while the other world's renewal and append latency stay in bound.
- [ ] #5685 fairness-attack cases applicable to a spill host are run and recorded on this issue.
title: id: spill v2 phase 3 — multi-world spill admission control and fairness budgets (#5787)

## Multiplexed persistent streams over ONE tunnel for the sandbox↔laptop path (WS-C design, from #5701)

Part of epic #5412. Design evidence: WS-C connection-performance comment on #5701 (2026-11-04).

### Measured problem (2026-11-04, trips.jsonl n=1149 + live probes)
- Warm single trivial call: client trip p50 369 ms (status-200, <2 s subset, n=800) while daemon work is 1–11 ms (daemon trips.jsonl; example trip aedc705d4294: client 445 ms vs daemon 1 ms). Transport ≈ 99% of cost.
- The path is HTTP/1.1-request-per-call over a pooled CONNECT tunnel (pool 50 in `fleet proxy serve`). Even warm, one request/response costs ~170–600 ms over the runtime-proxy (:3130) + DERP hairpin path. A warm RTT is the floor for EVERY operation, and every CLI operation is a separate call.
- Cold CONNECT measured 1,434 ms trip (same-minute warm trip: 212 ms) — CONNECT setup ≈ 1.2–1.8 s, and the ramp test on #5701 showed CONNECT setup serializes under concurrency (128 tunnels = 14.6 s wall, no failures).
- Failure amplification: during proxy wobble, trips cluster at 502 after ~16.3 s (p50, n=119) and no-status after ~26 s (p50, n=73) — retry chains multiply the herd.

Replace HTTP-per-call over N pooled tunnels with ONE (or two, for redundancy) persistent tunnel carrying multiplexed streams:

title: Connection perf: multiplexed persistent streams over one tunnel (replace HTTP-per-call + pool of 50)

```
Checking runtime dependencies for awscli-1.44.21-py3-none-any.whl
  - botocore==1.42.31 not satisfied by version 1.43.79
  - s3transfer<0.17.0,>=0.16.0 not satisfied by version 0.19.2
```

awscli 1.44.21 pins botocore exactly and s3transfer to the 0.16 line, but every current pin (master/unstable/stable/25 alike) ships botocore 1.43.79 and s3transfer 0.19.2 — the tree is mid-transition (libraries bumped, awscli not yet). An overlay in `nixos/nixpkgs/default.nix` (next to the patchelf override) overrides `awscli` to use dedicated botocore 1.42.31 and s3transfer 0.16.0 derivations (the set's own expressions with version/source rolled back), leaving the set's botocore/s3transfer at their current versions for all other consumers (boto3 etc.).

Remove once stock awscli passes `pythonRuntimeDepsCheck` on the assigned set's pin — i.e. upstream nixpkgs bumps awscli to a release whose botocore/s3transfer requirements match the tree (or restor

## Summary

Replace the stdio half of mcpx's takeover handoff with **one supervisor per stdio instance**: a tiny process (the same mcpx binary re-executed as a hidden `mcpx supervise` subcommand) that spawns each stdio MCP server, owns its pipes for the child's whole life, and serves whichever daemon is currently attached over a unix socket in the state directory. A daemon upgrade then becomes a plain restart of the front end — the new daemon *attaches* to supervisors that are already running. No pipes move, no descriptors are passed, nothing is detached or restored.

## Summary

Expand #2046 (serverless edition — `id` on Cloudflare Workers) with the storage decision it left open: what is the backing store for `id` when it runs on Workers, and can the answer be more than one store?

This is a design investigation, not an implementation ticket. Its deliverable is a decision-ready comparison of **Cloudflare D1 vs Turso (libSQL) vs offering both**, a recommendation with the conditions that would flip it, and follow-on design tickets (see Decomposition sketch) detailed enough to be broken into implementation work without re-litigating the choice.

Relates to: #2046 (serverless edition on Cloudflare Workers), #806 (F12.13 journal replication — read replicas over a signed stream).

## Why this matters

The serverless edition promises `id` with no server to run. That promise lives or dies on the store underneath it:

- Every `id` invariant — identity, capability grants, journal / event history, world state — has to survive on a store whose consistency, replication, and failure model were designed for edge web apps, not necessarily for a signed, replicated journal.
- Picking the wrong store does not just cost performance; it can silently weaken the journal's guarantees (ordering, durability, replay) or lock the serverless edition into a cost / limits shape that only appears at scale.
- Conversely, supporting two stores doubles the storage-abstraction surface forever. "Both" must be justified, bounded, and priced — not adopted as an avoidance of de

Implements the accepted design from #2818. See the design note `doc/2026-11-01_design_id2818.md` and design PR #3875.

Build the journaled handoff for an application-owned entity crossing between spatial region shard-worlds. Use dedicated source/destination journal entries plus coordinator open/close records. The required local order is prepare/validate → persist typed record → apply in-memory state → acknowledge. Keep region journals independent; do not emulate a cross-region transaction or put entity payloads in the coordinator journal.

## Phased packets

1. **Journal/schema/checkpoint foundation** — typed handoff records, entity-addressed input, world journal version 3 bump/rollback compatibility, and compaction preservation for active handoffs, epochs, tombstones, and receipts.
2. **Program contract + source export/fence** — pure `prepare_entity_transfer` hook, region-sharded mode gate, complete bounded entity payload, persist-before-apply source record, and source-side stale-write rejection. No receipt until apply/replay succeeds.
3. **Destination import** — module/schema/digest validation, persist-before-apply import, idempotency by handoff ID, durable receipt only after apply/replay, and failure tests.
4. **Coordinator/recovery** — journal start and observed receipts, retry/reconcile after crashes, and region-map switch only after matching durable receipts and a durable completion record.
5. **Client/operations** — explicit transit/stuck status, fail-closed entity rea
