Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Supports the permission-UX design (statements S19–S23 of the 2026-11-04 brief); filed as its own research per Drew's rule that sub-parts with a lot of prior art get dedicated documentation even when not needed for V1.

## Task

Survey how existing platforms present and remember capability grants, and extract what works and what users actually understand:

- **Google Play** permission declarations and runtime permission groups (the brief's named model).
- **Android runtime permissions**: ask-on-first-use, per-permission memory, "ask every time," permission auto-reset for unused apps.
- **iOS** prompts and privacy nutrition labels.
- **Browser extension** permissions (Chrome/Firefox): install-time vs runtime host permissions, optional permissions.
- **OAuth scopes**: blanket vs incremental authorization, scope creep complaints.
- **OS sandbox prompts**: macOS TCC, Flatpak portals — per-resource, per-app remembered grants.
- Failure literature: permission fatigue, blanket-accept rates, why install-time-only lists failed on Android and were replaced.

## Deliverable

A research doc: per-system summary (what's shown, when, what's remembered, revocation), a comparison table, and a shortlist of patterns that fit a two-sided (client + server admin) grant model — feeding the permission-UX design child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955).

D

Filed by the design architect (pass 62, 2026-11-06), originating on the trigger recorded at pass 61: *a fifth fleet-proxy bound/validation surface files* — #6518 filed the same day, the `token_file` sibling of #6516 in the same function.

## Summary

The fleet proxy (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-proxy`) and its sibling client (`pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-dispatch`) read two kinds of values they do not control: request frames from local callers (`serve.rs parse_request`) and HTTP responses from laptop services (`http.rs`, `connect_udp.rs`, dispatch's `lib.rs`). ## Finding (from #1075 slice 1, queue task 1256)

`nixos-playwright-e2e` fails on a readiness race in its own VM test script: the first probe is a single non-retried `curl` against a server that is not up yet.

**Evidence:** `id e2e nightly` run [40457980141](https://github.com/developing-today/code/actions/runs/40457980141) on `main` @ `dd4ee06e13393df7d6f2f0ccc72ffd2f5d36e865`, concluded failure 2026-10-27T07:51:41Z:

- ❌ `checks.x86_64-linux.nixos-playwright-e2e` — builder failed exit code 1. Traceback in `vm-test-run-id-playwright-e2e`:
  ```
  File "<string>", line 17, in <module>
    chromium_client.succeed("curl -sf http://chromium_server:4173/")
  RequestedAssertionFailed: command `curl -sf http://chromium_server:4173/` failed (exit code 7)
  ```
  Exit code 7 = connection refused. The failure fired ~53s after the VMs started (07:31:31Z → 07:32:24Z), while the server VMs were still booting / the app was still starting (pkarr/DNS publish noise in the same window). There is no `wait_for_open_port` / retry before the `succeed(...)` probe in the failing script path.

Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S36–S38 and S45 of the 2026-11-04 brief. This is the V3 stage of the program.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

User-level code should be passable into a **running world without recompiling the whole world**:

- At least in one version of the compiler there is a way to make a **DLL**. The **server side compiles that DLL itself** — user code is never trusted pre-compiled.
- The platform then **places the DLL in the appropriate location** for the world-side code to call it.
- If a user changes what's running, the world-side code **picks it up as soon as it's compiled and available to be hot-swapped in**.
- **Trust chain:** the server can trust the code because it did the compilation itself; and the only non-pure things the user function can do are from the **server's own platform being passed to it by the world author** — and the world author can trust that chain too.

## Design points to settle

- Interface contract: what signature/shape a user DLL exposes, and how the world discovers and binds it (name, version, interface hash). Mismatch behavior: refuse, fall back to previous version, or run the user's prior published code (see the compile-economics child — "keep running what you'd already published" is the stated default).
- Swap semantics: swap at tick boundary only? In-flight calls finish on the old code — state handoff between versions (the function's state is

## Problem

Queue task 18533 (for #7709) was quarantined by the claim path: its `payload.dedupe` lacks `checked_at`/`basis` (validation #5444), so every claim re-quarantines it. `quarantine-recheck` diagnoses it (`still_quarantined`, with that `last_error`) but cannot fix it, and **no verb repairs a task payload in place**. The only disposition available was cancel-with-disposition (done 2026-11-23; full record on #13091). The blocked pool likely contains more rows in this class — rows that read as "blocked" but are actually quarantined malformed packets.

What exists today (verified against the b8bbcc0 binary's `fleet queue --help`): `unblock` (incl. `--drop-dep`), `quarantine-recheck` (diagnose only), `revive`, `cancel`, `verify-disposition`, `dep-recheck`. None of them mutates a payload to fix a validation defect.

## Ask: `fleet queue repair <task-id> [--dry-run]`

A broker-side verb, sibling to `unblock`:

- Loads the task by id in whatever non-terminal state it sits in (blocked/quarantined; cancelled stays `revive`'s job — repair composes with revive, it does not replace it).
- Runs the packet validators and lists every defect it finds.
- Applies deterministic, semantics-preserving repairs for known defect classes. First class, the #7709 shape: a dedupe payload missing `checked_at`/`basis` is repaired by **re-performing the dedupe check live** — verify no other live task carries the same (repo, issue, kind) work identity — and stamping `checked_at`/`basis` recording tha

## Summary

Two related questions from the notes. First: can a Go module be made accessible to C — and what would that mean for mcpx, whose entire implementation currently lives under `internal/` and is therefore not importable even from Go. Second: `support embedding/config/dynamic-add mcp endpoints, connect to self over sockets?` — the daemon serving itself, or another mcpx, as an upstream MCP server.

The short answers: Go-to-C works, in two build modes, with real constraints, and it is the *third* thing to build, not the first — the ordering is public Go package → C ABI → WASM, and each step is only worth taking if the one before it has a caller. Self-composition works today in principle and needs a loop guard and an identity before it is safe to recommend.

## Original notes

> - can i make a go module accessible c
> - support embedding/config/dynamic-add mcp endpoints, connect to self over sockets?

## Current state (what mcpx does today, with file refs)

**There is no public Go API at all.** `cmd/mcpx/main.go` is 204 lines that import `internal/cli` and `internal/daemon`; every other package is under `internal/`, which the Go toolchain forbids any other module from importing. So today "embed mcpx in a Go program" me
title: mcpx: embedding mcpx -- a public Go API, the C ABI, WASM, and mcpx as its own upstream

Program epic. Drew ruled **"b and c"** on 2026-11-04 (dezren39/hatch-personal#21): Atlas search ships as **(b)** a Rust binary vendored from this repo and **(c)** a multi-client search service built on that binary.

**Design of record:** `doc/2026-11-04T08-07-13Z_design_atlas_binary_service/` (PR #5348, merged `9c5976340`). Read it before working any step — the decisions below are summaries, the note is the authority.

**Headline decisions**
- One Rust binary (`atlas-search`, `pkgs/atlas-search/`), two modes: standalone-capable one-shot CLI + `serve`. Never thin-client-only.
- Service protocol: HTTP+JSON jobs; branch workers concurrent; fused rankings in an in-memory TTL temp store behind per-job capability tokens; fetch-to-fill escalation lives inside the vector branch, paging slices an immutable ranking.
- Auth: per-client bearer tokens in `~/.local/state/atlas-search/service.json`, each carrying a **maximum sensitivity ceiling the server clamps to**. Named clients only; Aster is not a v1 client. Loopback + tailscale serve (MagicDNS), never public.
- Vector backend is a pluggable strategy (`scan` / `index-fill` / `index-fixed`); the golden-311 A/B running on the Python decides the default (design Gate C).
- The Python CLI stays the eval reference permanently and the runtime fallback through cutover. Migration is additive-first; there is no data migration (the system is read-only end to end).

**Program gates** (design §5): Gate A embedder bit-identity on the probe set; Gate
title: Epic: Atlas as a Rust binary + multi-client search service (b+c)

## Where it stands
The app is served from the Worker `pm-console-edge` (pm-stack/console/edge). With the laptop away it still opens, shows the last state the laptop reported (marked with its age), holds twelve kinds of action for the laptop's return, and sends notifications. It cannot read anything fresh or act at once: every read and write of the queue store and of GitHub still happens on the laptop.

## What is wanted
While the laptop has not reported for about a minute, the edge reads and acts by itself where nothing on the laptop is needed:
- reads: the board (queue store), pull requests, ranked issues, the owner's prompts and their replies (GitHub);
- writes that are one call: reply to or close a prompt, comment, rank an issue, move a task;
- a new prompt: the issue is one call, but its queue task goes through `fleet queue enqueue`, which is the fleet binary. Either the edge writes the task by the queue's documented contract, or the issue is filed and marked so the laptop enqueues it on return. Decide from `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-queue` and doc/agents/one-queue-claiming-work.md, not by copying SQL blind.

## Design already worked out
- `Ops` and `Work` (pm-stack/console/src) take a `run` function and a `fetch`. `Ops.gh` only ever runs `fleet gh api [-X M] <path> [--input -]`, and the queue store is already reached by `fetch`. An edge `run` that turns those argv into GitHub REST calls, and `fleet secrets get <queue token name>` into a Worker secret, lets both classes run
title: pm-console edge: do queue and GitHub operations from Cloudflare while the laptop is away

Parent: #176

## Summary

`mcpx exec` runs a script and returns what it produced. This asks for the caller to be able to attach natural-language instructions to the *edges* of that run — before it, after it, on failure, on success — so the deterministic script stays deterministic and the fuzzy parts sit outside it.

That is a better factoring than it first appears. The script is the part that must be reproducible; "make sure these dependencies exist wherever this runs" and "clean up the results and transform them" are the parts that legitimately vary by environment and by caller. Keeping them out of the script means the same script file works everywhere and the variation is in the *options*, which is exactly the shape `ExecOptions` was designed for (#40, step 7: "not a new method, an option").

## Original notes

> - mcp-owned opencode api support
>   - accept prompt/prePrompt/postPrompt/onErrorPrompt/onSuccessPrompt
>     - the script interface just runs the scripts, but you can provide a prePrompt saying hey i added a bunch of dependencies please make sure they exist where the job runs, postPrompt to clean up the results and transform, either prompt/pre/post could say to fix error thing but onError gets provided above or below the er
title: mcpx: lifecycle hooks on exec — prePrompt/postPrompt/onError as one declared list, script or prompt, with a declared effect

Implements §7.3 of the #2025 review-loop design (`files/review-loop-design-2025.md`, linked from #2025).

The fleet monitor already reconciles queue↔GitHub divergence hourly; the review loop adds three checks to that duty, all **report-only** at Stage B:

1. **Verdict without packet** — a verdict agent-note or `review/second-pass` label with no live second-pass (or interim-form) packet → protocol gap, handled like protocol §6.4(a).
2. **Count divergence** — label pass ≠ packet payload `review.pass` ≠ latest verdict footer → flag and repair from the payload (authoritative), noting the repair.
3. **Stale pass** — a commissioned pass unclaimed past normal claim latency, or a pass artifact unverdicted past its effort-class deadline → tracker flag in `assigned-tracker.md`, as for any assigned item.
Plus: a `review/*` label surviving issue closure is a finding (the artifact left the loop without a terminal verdict, design §7.4).

**Acceptance**
- [ ] All three checks run in the hourly monitor pass and appear in its run summary only when they fire
- [ ] A planted divergence (test issue with mismatched label/payload pass) is detected and repaired from the payload
- [ ] No check takes a non-report action at Stage B

Parent: #2025 · Design: review-loop-design-2025.md §7.3 · Depends on the schema follow-up (pass payload) and the label follow-up landing first.
title: review loop: fleet-monitor checks for verdict/packet reconciliation (design #2025 §7.3)

Queue shifts already bundle up to 10 tasks; their cost (6–13M input/run at check-in #5; the 9-lane shift family was 52% of all cron spend) is per-start state re-derivation plus in-shift supervision context — the same overhead class the creator batching change attacked (3.93M → ~1.4M input per filed issue).

Do:
1. Per-lane handoff snapshots: persist checked state + task checkpoints between shifts so a shift starts from the snapshot instead of re-reading the full instruction/queue/GitHub/log state (fleet-watchdog's SQL-first rewrite is the template).
2. Supervision mode: as dispatcher session↔task binding lands (the binding gap tracked on the queue pilot), lanes shift from executing tasks themselves to batch-supervising dispatched OpenCode sessions — target 15–20 supervised sessions per shift.
3. Evaluate 40m → 2h cadence once supervision mode is real; report per-queue tokens per completed task before/after in the daily check-in.
title: Shift batching, creator-style: lane handoff snapshots + supervision mode for queue lanes

Found by the 2026-11-14 whole-PM-stack backup/DR audit (verdict issue filed same day).

**Observed (2026-11-14, laptop amd):**
- The code repo's `.sops.yaml` names two age recipients: `laptop-framework` = `age125acas5y8hnwl5uhcp364xm8zlhtwsjqvxxpge8k04dzzr67acrq0ttc34` and `claude-sandbox`.
- `age-keygen -y ~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt` on the laptop returns exactly the `laptop-framework` public key — the laptop's SOPS private key lives only in that one file (75 bytes, dated 2024-10-14).
- That file is in **no** backup set: `laptop-state-backup` covers only `~/.local/state/opencode`, `~/secrets/*.sops.yaml`, `~/.ssh`; `agent-backup` is local-only and does not list it; no other routine names it.
- The fleet secrets list (Bitwarden Secrets Manager, names only) contains `sops.age-private-key-sandbox` — the **sandbox** key — and no laptop/framework age key at all.

**Consequence:** the SOPS ciphertext is backed up (`~/secrets/*.sops.yaml` rides laptop-state-backup, and the `.sops.yaml` files are in git), but if the laptop disk dies, nothing can decrypt the laptop-recipient files on a new machine. The encrypted backups are then dead weight for every secret that is encrypted to the laptop recipient only.

**Fix shape:** store the laptop age private key by name in Bitwarden Secrets Manager (value never in git/chat), and/or add `~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt` to the laptop-state restic set; verify by decrypting one laptop-recipient SOPS file in a scratch dir using only the vault-retriev
title: SOPS decryption key not recoverable

**Events, as supported per environment:**
- mouse enter / mouse leave
- click

Drew's order (2026-11-13, main chat): in addition to using Whisper directly from the Cloudflare models, add Whisper (speech-to-text) and TTS into the OpenCode config, supporting routing pools, auto failover, and proper proxying to the model — possibly a pool for both directions.

Scope:
- Transcription models (Whisper family) and speech models (MeloTTS family) become first-class routable models in the OpenCode config, addressable through route pools like text models are today.
- Pools for both directions: a speech-to-text pool and a text-to-speech pool; evaluate one combined speech pool covering both directions and pick the shape that keeps direction/capability gating clean.
- Auto failover across providers carrying these models (Cloudflare Workers AI first; any other provider in the catalog carrying the same models joins as another door), with the standing routing rules (a 100%-walled leg is not attempted; failure skips to the next leg inside the same request).
- Proper proxying to the model: audio payloads pass through the route layer intact, with per-provider format translation where providers differ (the capabilities supplement's per-provider input-variance rule applies to audio too).
- Automatic silence removal in the OpenCode path as well as the Cloudflare-direct path: audio is trimmed / voice-activity-detected before transcription so silence is not billed or transcribed; for TTS, generated-audio duration is what is billed, so nothing extra is synthesized.
- Capability
title: OpenCode: Whisper STT + TTS as routed pool models — failover, proxying, silence auto-trim

## Summary

"Tell mcpx to do a thing and it tries its best" — administration by intent rather than by remembering which of sixty operations does what.

Most of the specific operations listed in the note already exist, and the ones that do not should be built as **ordinary declared operations first**, because the ops table is the thing that makes them reachable from every surface at once. The prompt layer on top is then a router from a sentence to an operation, not an interpreter that invents behaviour — which also answers the note's own parenthetical, "(same interface for this and clients? plugins?)": mcpx already solved that, and the answer is the ops table.

The second bullet — provisioning arbitrary languages, tools and repositories — is a genuinely different and much larger problem, and is treated separately below.

Scope (from the handoff doc's MTC analysis): Cloudflare Merkle Tree Certificates authenticate a batch checkpoint with an inclusion proof per certificate; they can remove repeated CA signatures from the handshake when the client holds fresh authenticated landmarks — they do NOT remove the leaf key or the TLS handshake signature. Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Statements S17–S18 of the 2026-11-04 brief.

## Requirement (Drew, in substance)

Design the system for when a place a user has **already connected to before** changes its capabilities:

- The change may be an **expansion** (strict superset), or a **sideways modification** — not a strict reproduction of the previous capability set.
- **By default there is a warning or notice before the user connects** and has unexpected results. No silent upgrades of what a known world can do.

## Design points to settle

- What is compared: the registry's requested set, the discovered-used set (see the capability-model child of [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955)), or both? A change in *used* with no change in *requested* is exactly the sideways case that matters.
- Notice content: diff presented in plain language (new capabilities named), not a hash change.
- User choices on notice: proceed once, proceed and accept the new set as the baseline, refuse. Is there a "remember for capability decreases only" asymmetry (decreases are safe, increases warn)?
- Who else gets notified: server admins for server-side capabilities, world authors when a library they depend on changes its capability footprint.
- Interaction with invites ([#5751](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5751)): does accepting an invite pin the capability set the invite was issued under?

## Rela
title: id: design: capability-change notices on reconnect — expansion and sideways changes

## Direction (Drew, 2026-10-31)

Atlas moves from a single canonical DB + one Turso publish to provenance-first, scalable infrastructure. Design doc: hatch-personal `workspace/turso-atlas/docs/atlas-provenance-and-scale-design-2026-10-31.md`.

Rules:
1. Keep ALL data — nothing stripped from atlas.db or publishes to save space; only byte-identical dupes are cleaned, backups kept.
2. Backups AND plain extracts for every corpus.
3. Every chunk records EVERY place it was found: `chunk_occurrences` (chunk → array of source locators with spans, observed_at). Today dedup silently drops occurrences (~127K at first ingest); 6,344 canonical sessions own zero chunks for exactly this reason and their occurrences are unrecorded.
4. Every import is interned content-addressed (laptop extracts CAS / R2, registry maps CA hash → normal paths) or pinned as `repo@commit:path`. Registry also holds line numbers / dates / spans for extracts.
5. Retrieval: vector/FTS search across multiple Turso shard DBs (collection × month) returns IDs; a catalog/registry resolves an ID to a file, a chunk, or a start–end section — including a member of a tar in R2 (sidecar index, range fetch) or a local file.

Verified state feeding this (2026-10-31): canonical 18,325 sessions / 122,124 messages / 107,639 chunks; local-only = 6,941 chunks of personal-client TEXT held back from Turso by policy (not missing embeddings); Turso atlas 1.0 GB / 100,698 chunks; laptop ~/atlas 12 GB contains NO consequential byte-identica

design: bake the SSH recovery path into the fleet binary

Links: epic #5412 · laptop-agent design #5343
Drew's end state: **no shell scripts, no Python scripts — just the fleet
binary.** This issue covers the *recovery* SSH path only (the daemon-down
escape hatch). The everyday path's Python is the sibling item: the
`fleet laptop-agent` client domain (see Ordering, below).

## Context — the recovery path today (three of our files)

`~/tools/laptop-ssh.sh` (the shim) delegates exec-style calls to the
laptop-agent, but shapes the agent cannot express fall back to real SSH.
The fallback classes, from the shim's own header:

- `LAPTOP_SSH_REAL=1` (explicit escape hatch / daemon-down recovery)
- no arguments (interactive session) or a **leading ssh option**
  (`-L/-R/-W/-N/-t/-p/-l/-i/-o …` — forwards and TTY allocation)
- **stdin carrying data** for the remote command (sudo -S feeds,
  `cat > file` pushes) — the daemon has no stdin channel

The fallback is `~/tools/laptop-ssh-real.sh`, which `exec`s system ssh:

```sh
exec ssh \
  -o "ProxyCommand=python3 $HOME/tools/laptop-proxy-connect.py" \
  -o "StrictHostKeyChecking=yes" \
  -o "UserKnownHostsFile=$HOME/.ssh/known_hosts_laptop" \
  -o "IdentitiesOnly=yes" -i "$HOME/.ssh/id_ed25519" \
  -o "ConnectTimeout=60" -o "ConnectionAttempts=3" \
  -o "ServerAliveInterval=15" -o "ServerAliveCountMax=8" \
  -o "ControlMaster=auto" -o "ControlPath=$HOME/.ssh/cm-%r@%h:%p" \
  -o "ControlPersist=3600" \

archer-slack-review polls a watermark every 15 min (~100K input/run × ~96 runs/day ≈ 9.6M/day) and usually finds nothing. Replace the polling with an event-driven collector (Drew approved 2026-10-29):

Found during the 2026-11-07 fleet-wide DB audit + rename/mode-fix program (#6619).

Facts, all empirically verified on scratch DBs (CLI v1.0.33):
- `turso db list` TYPE column is the only mode evidence: `SQLite` = libsql mode, `Turso` = TursoDB mode.
- There is no `turso db rename`.
- A `--from-db` fork INHERITS the source database's type; `turso db create --from-db X --tursodb` fails with "tursodb flag contradicts the database derived type". A fork can never change mode.
- The only working conversion is: `turso db export <db>` -> copy the export files to the target basename -> `turso db import <file>.db --tursodb` (the new DB is named after the FILE basename), then repoint every producer, confirm, and delete the old DB.
- `turso db dump` does not exist in this CLI version (prints help).

Impact: converting the fleet's 8 libsql DBs on 2026-11-07 meant 8 full data moves (~7.7 GB total exports), per-DB token re-mints, and producer flips — for what should be a metadata operation. If Turso ever ships a mode-convert or rename verb, the fleet's remaining libsql holdouts (atlas monolith, great-star-lord — both deliberately untouched, see #6619) should use it. Until then, any new fleet DB must be created with --tursodb at birth; a libsql DB created by accident costs a full migration later.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The rule 'every new fleet Turso DB is created with --tursodb at birth' is recorded in the fleet's DB-creation documentation/runbook where a creator will see it.

title: turso CLI: no rename and no libsql->TursoDB mode conversion — every fix is a full export/import data move

## Problem: home IPv6 uplink stalls on real transfers

Diagnosed 2026-10-26 during the OpenClaw install work on the amd laptop.

**Symptom:** IPv6 connections to Cloudflare-fronted hosts (e.g. registry.npmjs.org) stall at zero bytes on payload-sized responses, while IPv4 to the same hosts is healthy (~530 KB/s).

Evidence (on amd, home network):
- `curl -6` of a ~4 MB npm tarball: 0 bytes after ~22 s (hard stall, not slowness).
- `curl -4` of the same tarball: full download in ~8 s.
- Interactive tools with happy-eyeballs (curl default) mask the problem by falling back to IPv4; node/pnpm does not fall back the same way, so nix fixed-output fetches for npm/pnpm deps repeatedly stalled mid-build (notably the ~780-package summarize pnpm-deps FOD), while shell tests looked fine.

## Impact

- npm/pnpm fetches from Nix builds on home machines are unreliable/slow.
- Any IPv6-first client without robust fallback can hang on this network.

## Workaround in place

- IPv4 precedence via `networking.getaddrinfo` in the amd host config (precedence ::ffff:0:0/96 = 100), marked as temporary.
- Prefer-IPv4 choices in ad-hoc tooling until this is fixed.

## What "fixed" means

Find and repair the root cause on the home network. Suspects, in order:
1. PMTUD black hole on the IPv6 path (large packets dropped; small handshakes succeed — matches the 0-byte-after-connect shape).
2. Router/ONT IPv6 handling (prefix delegation, RA/MTU advertisement, firmware).
3. ISP IPv6 routing/peering toward Clo
title: Home network: IPv6 uplink stalls on payload transfers (PMTUD/router/ISP)

Part of epic #1184 (PM stack coherence — wave 2, 2026-10-26).

The PM stack's failure modes are silent by default: a dead collector, an aged feed, a rejected orchestration section, or a down service have all presented as "everything is fine" at least once (#1110 being the worked example). Health pages and watchdogs only help if they actually fire — and that is only ever tested by accident. Scheduled chaos/rotation drills make it deliberate: on a cadence, a drill injects one known fault (kill the fleet-feed collector, artificially age the feed, drop one component service, corrupt one feed section), then verifies the expected signals fire — the degraded banner on the affected pages, the watchdog entry in NEEDS ORCHESTRATOR, the health page state — and files the drill result automatically as an issue comment (or a new issue when a signal does NOT fire). Drills run against the deployed stack in a maintenance window, restore everything they touched, and never run two faults at once.

Acceptance:
- A documented drill schedule exists (at least collector-kill, feed-aging, and one service-drop), runnable on demand and on cadence.
- Each drill verifies named expected signals (banner / watchdog / health state) and records pass/fail per signal.
- A failed signal files an issue automatically under epic #1184 with the drill evidence attached; a passed drill posts its result to the tracking issue.
- Drills restore all touched state (verified by a post-drill health read) and are interlocked
title: design(pm-stack): chaos/rotation drills — scheduled game-days (kill collector, age the feed, drop a service) verifying banners, watchdogs, and self-healing fire

## Context

The 2026-11-04 nixpkgs update (tracking: #2715) moves `nixpkgs-25` `e7439b6b` -> `1d060086` (the Hydra-gated nixos-unstable channel revision). At the new revision, `haskellPackages.regex-pcre` (pulled into the amd system closure via `haskellPackages.misfortune` in `nixos/environment/default.nix`) is marked broken under nixpkgs' problems framework, and the marking is honest: with the broken flag warned through, its build fails deterministically in the configure phase --

```
Error: [Cabal-7620]
The program 'pkg-config' version >=0.9.0 is required but it could not be found.
```

nixpkgs' Haskell builder no longer adds the `pkg-config` wrapper (or the pkgconfig-depends libraries) to Haskell build environments -- the same mechanism the 2026-10-30 run hit on the master pin (that instance is tracked in #3906). Drew ruled on 2026-11-04 ("fix it or pin misfortune") to revive the #3906-class override for the nixpkgs-25 segment rather than keep the input frozen.

## The temporary override

`nixos/environment/default.nix` extends the raw `nixpkgs-25` legacyPackages segment with an overlay that overrides `haskellPackages.regex-pcre` to append `pkg-config` to its `nativeBuildInputs` and a minimal vendored pcre 8.45 (the version the old pins shipped; test suite disabled) to its `buildInputs`, restoring the old build environment for this one package. A problems handler scoped to `regex-pcre` warns the broken marking through so the overridden derivation can evaluate.

## Removal

# design: versioning for a monorepo whose apps deploy individually

**WS-H** · Design task (survey + interim policy), filed 2026-11-04. Related: epic #5765 (deployment architecture — services layer + deploy tool), #5766 (deploy tool v1), #5760 (fleet Nix-build state; the deployed-lag table that motivates this), PR #5764 (the services-layer design).

## Why

Under the NixOS system closure, "what version is running" was declarative: the system profile *was* the answer. The services-layer design (#5764) deliberately takes apps out of that closure so they can deploy individually — which buys deploy/rollback flexibility and sells the free identity answer. #5760 shows the failure mode already, before any of that lands: the deployed fleet binaries lag `pkgs/fleet` HEAD by five commits — including a proxy request-line validation hardening — and nothing noticed, because every one of those commits self-reports the same version string, `0.1.0`. A hand-maintained version constant does not move when code moves.

Drew's counter-measures (2026-11-04): every binary **self-reports** an embedded version (number + git hash) via `--version`/`--about` or its version verb; versions are **derived automatically** from tags + branch state so no two builds ever collide; monorepo releases use **per-app prefixed tags** for what was actually tested and shipped, **plus a whole-repo tag** for the commit; the numbers are **technically semver, loosely followed** — the constraint that matters is Rust consumer
title: design: versioning for a monorepo whose apps deploy individually — derived versions, per-app tags + repo date tag, survey of schemes (WS-H)

Extends #2048 (Zettelkasten layer — multiplayer docs/wiki on ID). This is an EXPANSION design and explicitly **a design to go make designs**: a feature-matrix investigation program whose output is a family of follow-on designs, not one monolithic spec.

## Problem

#2048 establishes the zettelkasten/knowledge layer on ID. Before building further, we need to know — systematically, not anecdotally — what the mature knowledge tools actually do, which of those features cluster into coherent ID designs, and how existing users' content gets in and out. Skipping this risks reinventing a worse Notion while missing the one feature (e.g. the graph, or daily notes) that makes a knowledge tool sticky.

## Method (the program itself)
1. **Enumerate:** for each product below, produce a feature inventory from primary sources (docs, hands-on use): features named consistently so they can be compared across products.
2. **Matrix:** build a product × feature matrix (products as columns, features as rows, with notes on quality/implementation differences, not just yes/no).
3. **Cluster:** group features into coherent clusters; each cluster becomes **one follow-on design ticket** against #2048.
4. **Decide per cluster:** adopt / adapt to ID's multiplayer object model / explicitly reject with reasons. No feature is adopted by default just because a competitor has it.
5. **Import/export designs** (below) proceed in parallel — they depend on the object model in #2048, not on every cluster decision.
title: id: design: Knowledge layer feature program — competitor feature matrix, import/export, read-authority

## Symptom
After the laptop's 2026-11-16 ~05:35–05:39 CT outage and recovery, `gnome-keyring-daemon` restarted (05:38) outside a desktop login session and stayed **locked**. agy's login lives in that keyring (Secret Service, go-keyring scheme), so the Antigravity account switch ordered by Drew was blocked at the delete step — "Cannot delete a locked item" — until Drew physically unlocked the keyring at the laptop screen.

## Why it should not happen
The keyring normally unlocks via PAM at desktop login. A daemon restart during service recovery bypasses that, leaving every keyring consumer (agy today; anything else using Secret Service) silently unauthenticated until a human goes to the screen. Drew's position: "it should unlock itself."

## Scope

- Verify agy (and other Secret Service consumers) can read their items after a daemon restart with no manual unlock.

## Acceptance check
Restart gnome-keyring-daemon out-of-session (simulating the recovery path), then confirm `agy --print` authenticates with no unlock prompt and no manual step.

## Design + build: `fleet connect` — explicit transport selection, sessions, and drop semantics

Origin: Drew's questions, 2026-11-14. Epic: #5412. Builds on #5343
(laptop-agent), #5697 (`fleet proxy ssh`), #5972 (fallback connection
mode), and the session semantics of the file-transfer build (sibling
issue filed the same day).

### Verified current state (2026-11-14) — what Drew asked to confirm

Three ways to reach the laptop exist today, chosen by *which tool you
invoke*, not by a flag:

1. **Agent exec** (`laptop-agent.py`, the day-to-day path; the Rust
   `fleet laptop-agent` domain is still a registry stub — exit 69,
   "implementation lands in a later step of epic #5412"). Commands run
   as argv directly on the laptop, **no shell** unless `--shell` is
   passed (then a login `bash -lc`). Environment is the daemon's
   systemd-user-service environment (plus the login profile under
   `--shell`) — nothing from the caller's environment crosses. **There
   is no stdin channel at all**: interactive input during a run is
   impossible on this path, which is exactly why stdin-carrying shapes
   fall back to SSH. Transport is HTTP over pooled CONNECT tunnels
   through the session proxy (warm call ~0.39–0.45 s; cold CONNECT

Execution issue for tracked goal **CPU/memory load over time + parallelism efficiency** (goal_8c75ed164542). Filed 2026-11-07 on Drew's ruling that the census "dead" goals were dormant because the fleet never ran work against them.

## Question

What concurrency level makes the sandbox VM (and the laptop executors) finish the most work per credit? Drew's framing: CPU near 99% because it's performing at peak is the target — 95% while 35 things complete beats 8-vs-6 things grinding the whole box to a halt. Find the concurrency sweet spot **empirically**, then fold the answer into delegation/orchestration practice.

## Plan

- [ ] Baseline: load profile snapshot (done — first comment on this issue, 2026-11-07 18:49 CST)
- [ ] Sampled profile over time: load average, run-queue depth, CPU user/sys/idle/iowait/steal, memory + swap pressure, sampled across busy and quiet windows (not just one evening snapshot)
- [ ] Concurrency sweep: run controlled parallel work at several lane/agent concurrency levels and measure completed-work throughput + latency degradation per level
- [ ] Identify the noisy-neighbor cliff: the level where context-switch / iowait / steal growth eats the gains
- [ ] Write the delegation battle plan: who orchestrates, how work is tracked, concurrency defaults per machine, coordination-chatter budget
- [ ] Fold the defaults into the orchestration / lane runbooks so the finding changes behavior, not just this issue

## Acceptance

- [ ] A measured sweet-spot number
title: investigate: CPU/memory load over time + parallelism sweet spot on the sandbox VM

## Summary

mcpx has at least seven TTLs across five subsystems, and **none of them can be renewed**. Every one is
absolute from creation, so a caller that is still working, still watching, or still waiting for a person
loses the thing anyway. The fix should be one convention applied everywhere, not a `renew` endpoint per
resource type.

## Original notes

> - elicit/prompt/session/attachment/mcp/etc renew ttl

## Current state (what mcpx does today, with file refs)

| resource | setting | default | how the deadline is computed | renewable |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| elicitation question | `elicit.ttl` (a built-in default, **not** a registry setting -- see below) | **120s** | `ExpiresAt = Created + ttl` (`internal/elicit/elicit.go:206`; also `internal/daemon/hooks.go:145,198`) | no |
| task result | `tasks.ttl`, per-task `ttl` in ms | 10m | `time.AfterFunc(ttl, …)` armed once at `Start` (`internal/tasks/tasks.go:104-147`) | no |
| artifact | `artifacts.ttl`, per-put override | 24h | `Expires: now.Add(ttl)` (`internal/artifacts/artifacts.go:303-317`) | no |
| interruptible call (`/v1/ask`) | `proto.askTTL` | 15m | absolute (`internal/settings/proto.go:66`) | no |
| resumable request state | `proto.stateTTL` | 30m |
title: mcpx: one convention for renewing TTLs -- touch-on-read, not a renew endpoint per resource

## Summary

Two programmes in one design, because they share infrastructure and each is half as useful without the other:

1. **A denial-of-service test suite in CI** — adversarial load and abuse coverage that runs continuously, extending #560 (F12.18 DoS test suite in CI) from a test-suite idea into a full adversarial programme.
2. **A performance benchmark programme** — repeatable, comparable benchmarks of a standard server and of advanced scaling techniques, per interface, run as **regression gates, not one-offs**.

Relates to: #560.

## Why both, why together

- A system can pass benchmarks and still fall over under adversarial traffic; it can survive abuse and still be unusably slow for honest users. The load-generation, measurement, and environment machinery is largely the same — designing them separately duplicates it and guarantees the two suites drift into incomparable numbers.
- Benchmarks without gates decay into dashboard decoration. DoS tests without baselines cannot distinguish "attack worked" from "server was already slow." Each programme supplies what the other lacks.

## Part 1 — DoS / adversarial load suite (extends #560)

### Threat and load classes to cover

- **Connection-level abuse:** slow clients (slowloris-style), connection floods, half-open churn, oversized / never-ending requests, rapid reconnect storms.
- **Request-level abuse:** expensive-query amplification, large payload / blob abuse, decompression and parsing bombs within protocol limits, requ

Part of the worlds design program: [#5955](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5955). Wave-2 follow-up from the prior-art research (Lane B item 20); parent topic issue: [#5964](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5964). Research source: `workspace/scratch/worlds-capabilities-brief-2026-11-04/prior-art-research.md`.

## Precedent

**LambdaMOO feature objects** are the library model Drew described, working since the '90s: create a feature object implementing reusable verbs, and any player object can attach it and gain those commands — libraries as *runtime-attached objects*, no recompilation of the consumer (https://www.moo.mud.org/moo-faq/lcore-getting-started.html).

## Scope

Distinct from the taxonomy child of #5955 (attachment as *classification*: genre/game/entity/none) and from the DLL design (#5964: per-user *functions*): this is runtime attach/detach of *library behavior* to entities inside a running world.

- Attach/detach semantics: who may attach (entity owner, world author), at what moment (tick boundary), what happens to in-flight invocations.
- The attached library's capability footprint composes with the entity's and the world's ceilings — checked how, at attach time?
- Detach and version change: state the library accumulated on the entity — kept, migrated, dropped?

## Done looks like

A design note stating whether feature-object attachment is a v-next mechanism for us, and if so its semantics; if not, the recorded reason.
title: id: design: feature-object library attachment — runtime attach/detach of library behavior to entities without world recompilation

## User story

As the operator of our own services, I want one self-hosted identity provider issuing OIDC + SAML SSO for our own services — pm-stack, the mcpx and Desktop Commander doors ([#13404 — Desktop Commander front door endpoint](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13404)), OpenChamber, fleet surfaces — so that sign-in across our estate runs on our own identity instead of a patchwork of third-party IdPs and per-service arrangements.

Motivation:

- One identity: the same person, service, and policy across every service, instead of a separate account story per service.
- Our own trust anchor: signing keys and certificates issued from our own PKI, under our own control, instead of trusting a vendor's keys for our own estate.
- No per-service vendor dependency: adding a service means registering a relying party with our provider, not adopting another third-party IdP or inventing a one-off sign-in scheme.

Done at the story level looks like: our provider is the sign-in path for at least one service of each class in the acceptance criteria below, its signing keys come from our PKI and can be rotated without breaking sign-in, and a new service can be onboarded by configuration against our provider rather than by choosing a new identity vendor.

This story does not start from a blank page. It is the story-level frame over the SSO program that already exists — parent issue [#9077 — parent SSO program issue itself](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/907
title: story: our own OIDC/SAML/SSO identity provider

Extends #2036 (ID messaging/relay protocol v1). This is an EXPANSION design: it does not replace #2036, it defines the concrete wire format #2036 assumes and the adapter family that lets ID run where native iroh/UDP cannot.

## Problem

#2036 designs messaging/relay at the protocol level, but leaves open: (a) the exact bytes on the wire, (b) how ID traffic crosses interfaces that cannot natively speak the iroh UDP protocol, and (c) how relays/proxies behave as standard, high-performance infrastructure rather than ad-hoc fallbacks. Without a frozen wire contract, every adapter and every implementation invents its own framing and versioning, and forward compatibility becomes guesswork.

## Goal

One canonical postcard wire schema for ID, versioned and forward-compatible, plus a family of transport adapters that carry the *same* ID payloads unchanged over non-UDP interfaces, with relays and proxies specified as first-class standard protocols.

## Feature set — full expansion

### 1. Canonical postcard wire schema
- Define the exact postcard (serde / postcard crate) schema for every ID message type carried by #2036: envelope, handshake/identity, direct message, relayed message, control/keepalive, error, and capability negotiation.
- Envelope fields: schema major/minor, message type discriminator, sender/recipient IDs, stream/sequence identifiers, timestamp/clock fields, payload length, flags (compressed, encrypted, fragmented), and extension/TLV area.
- Serialization rules: field

Part of the Atlas family (#5755); follows #6788 (the per-query Durable Object search cache Worker, shipped with **indefinite retention — no TTL, no eviction — per Drew's explicit order for v1**).

Indefinite retention is the v1 contract, not an oversight. Before it becomes load-bearing at scale, the eviction policy needs a design pass. Nothing here is urgent; this issue exists so the questions are on the record rather than discovered later.

## Questions to settle

1. **Corpus invalidation.** The cache key pins the embedding space (model revision + vector table) and ceiling, so a re-embedding of the corpus (new model/table) naturally orphans old entries — they simply stop being keyed. But a re-ingest under the *same* space (chunk content changes, shards added/renamed) leaves stale results served forever. Is that acceptable for a personal-corpus search surface, or do we need a corpus-generation component in the key (e.g. a registry epoch the service reports), accepting that a generation bump cold-starts the whole cache?
2. **Growth bound.** Entries hold an embedding (~12 KB JSON) + result envelope (observed ~17 KB at k=3; larger at k=50). At personal query volumes this is small for a long time; still, is there a count/size ceiling after which LRU-by-`searched_at`/`hit_count` eviction (both already recorded per entry) should engage?
3. **Manual purge.** A gated purge route (per-key delete; maybe per-prefix) is cheap to add to the Worker — worth having from the start of any poli
title: Atlas search Worker cache: eviction & invalidation policy (follow-up to #6788)

## Task

Survey the existing machinery for machine-readable license identification so the classifier design doesn't invent a private format:

- **SPDX License List**: identifiers for every license in the brief's set (MIT and variants incl. MIT-0, BSD family, MPL-2.0, BlueOak-1.0.0, Apache-2.0, GPL-2.0/GPL-3.0/AGPL-3.0 with only/or-later distinctions, CC0-1.0, CC-BY-4.0, CC-BY-SA-4.0, CC NC variants), plus SPDX expressions for combinations (`MIT OR Apache-2.0`, `AND`) — the dual-licensing case our own standard (MIT or Apache) needs.

## Summary

Today a script that calls a tool wrongly fails at the wrong moment: the error arrives from a server, halfway through, after the side effects of every call before it. `--diagnose-preflight` (#41) fixed the statically-detectable half. This issue is the rest of it — a graded ladder of what mcpx does when a request is *probably* wrong, from "refuse it deterministically" through "ask the caller" to "rewrite it and run the rewrite", with the escalation policy as a setting rather than a hard-coded behaviour.

The unifying idea: **an execution outcome should be a structured verdict, not a boolean.** "It failed" loses the fact that eleven of twelve calls succeeded, which of them had side effects, what specifically was wrong with the twelfth, and what the minimal fix is. mcpx already computes most of those facts and throws them away.

title: mcpx: checking, refusing and repairing a request — a graded ladder from deterministic diagnostics to rewrite-and-run

## Idea

Record everything mcpx and its harness learn as events in one table, so that
any statistic is a query rather than a new code path.

Today `mcpx stats` has seven dimensions and `mcpx stats --opencode` has six,
each a hand-written query against a differently-shaped source. Adding a source
— a REST API, a hosted mcpx, a second harness — means writing that set again.

## Shape

```sql
CREATE TABLE event (
  id         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  ts_unix_ms INTEGER NOT NULL,
  kind_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES kind(id),
  idset_id   INTEGER REFERENCES idset(id),   -- who/what this concerns
  source     TEXT NOT NULL,                  -- mcpx, opencode, rest, tui
  value      REAL,                           -- the number, when there is one
  data       TEXT                            -- the rest, as JSON
);
```

### Identifier sets

The repeated shape is "this event concerns session X, whose parent is Y, in
worktree Z". Those combinations recur constantly, so interning them is both a
large space saving and what makes `GROUP BY idset_id` mean something.

CREATE TABLE idset (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, fingerprint TEXT UNIQUE);
CREATE TABLE idset_member (idset_id INTEGER, key TEXT, value TEXT,

## Summary

Implement spill v2 phase 2 from the #5787 design (`doc/2026-11-08_design_id5787.md`, §3): read replicas for a spilled world with an explicit staleness contract.

## Scope

- Replica read service over the authoritative journal stream: every read response carries the journal position it was served at (the replica's replay watermark).
- Bounded service: a replica beyond the configured lag bound refuses with retryable `replica-behind` instead of serving silently old state.
- Read-your-writes / monotonic reads: a client presenting its last acknowledged position is served only at a watermark ≥ that position (bounded wait or redirect to holder/DO).
- Presence rules: replicas may serve and originate only explicitly ephemeral, TTL'd, unjournaled presence data; session traffic that mutates goes to the holder and the append gate, always; no replica acknowledgment before the gate's durable receipt.

## Trigger / gating

**Do not start until trigger T2 fires:** the first production spill, or read load on a spilled world measurably served stale / refused at the holder. Design: #5787. Depends on: #3805, and on F1's pool/replica join (the phase-1 follow-on filed with the #5787 design).

## Acceptance

- [ ] Watermark, staleness-bound, and read-your-writes behaviours covered by deterministic tests, including the design §7 "replica serves during failover" case.
- [ ] No code path lets a replica acknowledge a mutation or promote presence data to durable state.
title: id: spill v2 phase 2 — read replicas with position-watermark staleness contract (#5787)

## Problem

When a model door stops answering, sessions routed to it stay wedged in a retry loop. They do not fail over to a door that works, and new waves keep being routed to the dead door. Five issues report the same failure, one per door, with 58 to 96 comments each and no code change:

| Issue | Door | Failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| #9549 | `_claude` | OAuth renewal answers 429; every session dies at launch |
| #9856 | `_antigravity` | 403, account disabled for terms of service |
| #9859 | `_muse` | 429, weekly window at 100% |
| #9961 | `cline-pass` | 429, monthly limit reached |
| #10085 | `opencode-go` sub-accounts | 429; sessions freeze at retry attempt 2 |

Each was parked on the owner. None needs him: a quota wall resets by itself, and what the fleet controls is whether it keeps sending work into the wall.

## What to build

1. **Measure first.** For each of the five doors, record today's state: answering, walled until a known reset time, or dead.
2. **A walled door is skipped until its reset.** When a door answers with a quota wall that names a reset time, or with an auth failure, the route marks the door unusable until that time (or until a probe succeeds) and stops routing new sessions to it.
3. **A wedged session fails over.** A session whose door fails this way moves to the next door in its route within one retry, or ends with a clear error that the scheduler can re-launch elsewhere. It does not hold a lane while it retries.
